MR. WOOLLIAMS  STATEMENTS BY PRIME MINISTER ON VIEWING OF FILM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I rise on a question of privilege that affects all members of the house. Not only does it affect all members of the house, but it reflects on what happened last Friday. The particular point of privilege which I raise today is this. With the greatest respect to the position he holds, I say that the Prime Minister has misinformed the house with reference to the film which has been discussed many times previously in this house.
I should like to read the answers to some questions which were put. I will give the dates to the Prime Minister and I should like him to follow me carefully. As reported at page 3429 of Hansard for May 21, 1964-I will leave out the first part of the questions because they do not go to the very root of my point of privilege-the Prime Minister was asked this question by the hon. member for Port Arthur:
In that event, Mr. Speaker, if it were possible for the production to be seen on some network other than the C.B.C., would the Prime Minister and his advisers give their approval for that to be done?

subtopic: TABLING OF INSTRUMENTS ADOPTED AT GENEVA MEETING

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: TABLING OF INSTRUMENTS ADOPTED AT GENEVA MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table the texts, in English and in French, of the instruments adopted at the international labour conference held in Geneva, Switzerland, and to make a brief explanation of the instruments. Its conclusions included one international labour convention and two recommendations.
The convention and one of the recommendations deal with the problem of the risk caused in industry by inadequately guarded machinery. They seek the prohibition of the sale, hire and use of inadequately guarded machinery. These were adopted at the conference without opposition. The provisions of these instruments are being taken into account in legislation now under active consideration in the occupational safety field.
The other recommendation deals with the principles and practices to be followed in relation to the termination of employment of workers at the initiative of the employer.
All of these instruments were supported by Canadian employer, worker and government delegates.
The constitution of the I.L.O. requires a member state to bring conventions and recommendations "before the authority or authorities within whose competence the matter lies for the enactment of legislation or other action". In the case of a federal state there is a further obligation to refer the instruments to the appropriate state or provincial authorities "for the enactment of legislation or other action", and to arrange for periodic

consultations with a view to promoting coordinated action to give effect to the provisions of the instruments.
The instruments will, therefore, in accordance with past practice, be brought officially to the attention of the provinces. My colleague the Secretary of State has sent copies to the lieutenant governor of each province, with the request that they be placed before the competent authority in the province for consideration.

[Editor's note: The answer referred to above is as follows:]
1.	Air Terminal Transport Limited have been granted the exclusive right and privilege to maintain and operate a limousine and taxi station at Toronto international airport for the operation of a limousine and taxi service, together with the right and privilege to park buses, limousines and taxis in connection with the operation at such locations to be determined by the airport manager.
2.	The department first entered into an agreement with Air Terminal Transport
Questions
Limited on August 1, 1951. The agreement was renewed in 1955 for five years; and again in 1960 for ten years, but at a higher rental.
3.	Carter Transportation Limited provided the previous ground transportation service at Toronto international airport. In accordance with the established policy of the department at the time, the air line operators serving the airport were permitted to select their own ground transportation carrier, following which the department negotiated with the carrier for an agreement to permit them to enter the airport to carry on their business. Carter Transportation Limited, having been selected by the air lines concerned, were granted a four year agreement by the Department of Transport effective August 1, 1947. Prior to the expiry of that term, the airlines concerned informed the department that they were not prepared to renew their agreement with Carter Transportation Limited, but instead wished to enter into an agreement with Air Terminal Transport Limited. Following negotiations between the department and Air Terminal Transport Limited, the Department of Transport agreed to grant them an agreement to serve the Toronto international airport, provided they first obtained the necessary public vehicle licence from the Ontario highway transport board. Air Terminal Transport Limited purchased the equipment of Carter Transportation Limited and subsequently the Ontario highway transport board, following public hearings, agreed to transfer Carter's public vehicle licence to Air Terminal Transport Limited.
4.	Other taxi operators are free to bring passengers to the airport, or to collect passengers at the airport by prearrangement. However, they may not solicit business at the airport, or pick up fares without prearrangement.
5.	Air Terminal Transport Limited is required to provide a 24 hour service at the airport to meet the needs of the airlines serving the airport and the travelling public. They are required to operate limousines, buses and special cars and to have them available in sufficient numbers at the airport to meet peak demands, both scheduled and unexpected, arising from weather delays, diversions, etc. They are required to provide modern equipment, to carry public liability insurance, and provide uniformed employees. All of this requires a very heavy capital investment on the part of the company, and to maintain such an investment it is necessary that the company

Questions
be given exclusive rights to the passenger traffic offerings at the airport. To permit unrestricted competition from taxis would make the whole operation economically unsound. Without granting the company exclusive rights, it would be impossible to provide the type of service required by the travelling public. Experience elsewhere indicates that ground transportation dependent on the chance availability of taxis at an airport would be most unsatisfactory. There might be an oversupply of taxis available during certain periods with objectionable efforts to compete for the available passengers. In bad weather when business might be brisk downtown there would be a shortage of vehicles at the airport, leaving passengers to wait long periods for transportation. A split concession as between limousines and taxis is also unworkable. The department tried such an experiment at another major airport and had to abandon it in favour of the single operator. There, taxis were competing with the limousine by soliciting group fares at the airport, or preceding the limousine to known hotel pick-up points, and again soliciting group fares.
6.	Air Terminal Transport Limited does not hold taxi licences. These are not required for the type of service performed by the company.
7.	Air Terminal Transport Limited holds public vehicle licence No. 1519 from the province of Ontario, which allows its vehicles to carry passengers to and from Toronto international airport, and to any point in the province of Ontario.
8.	The company operates 13 buses of the highway cruiser type. Eight are 41 passenger, and five are 33 passenger vehicles. Seven buses operate on a regular 15 minute service, and six are available for extra backup service. The company operates 90 late model sedans. These sedans are replaced with new ones every six months. An average of 55 cars are on duty at all times, 78 at peak periods, seven on the Hamilton service and five surplus at peak periods. The company's garage is located one half mile from the airport.

Inquiries of the Ministry with regard to the report in the press this afternoon that he has been in communication with the C.B.C., as was the Prime Minister on Friday last, relative to the film "Mr. Pearson" being shown to the Canadian public?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR SHOWING OF FILM RESPECTING PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have received the following letter from the president of the C.B.C.:
The corporation has been advised by the Prime Minister that in his personal view a television film known as "Mr. Pearson", rejected for broadcast by the C.B.C., should be given a public showing.
The corporation has also noted opinions expressed in the house by the Leader of the Opposition and other speakers.
The C.B.C. is responsible to parliament and must at all times carry out the wish and intent of parliament.
The independence of the C.B.C. from political influence in its operations is a cardinal point of public broadcasting policy. The corporation could not discharge its responsibility to parliament without this policy. Further, the public might well lose its confidence in the corporation and its program services if there were serious reason to doubt the corporation's integrity in such matters. Consequently, the corporation must at all times be careful not to confuse political matters with questions of broadcast responsibility.
With respect to the present situation it does not appear to the corporation that parliament has clearly indicated its wish that the rejected film be broadcast. In attempting to interpret the intent of parliament on this matter the corporation has encountered some difficulty.
This difficulty stems from the fact that since the inception of the C.B.C. it has been the custom of parliament to direct the work of the corporation only through approval of broadcasting policies in their broadest sense. The present instance is a question of whether or not a single program should be broadcast. Consequently there appears to be a question of principle or policy involved which may well transcend the more obvious and immediate considerations.
In the corporation's view this is a matter of great importance, keeping in mind the precedent that could be established in connection with broadcasting or showing of the film in question.
The corporation has already taken a broadcast decision with respect to this film. That decision was based solely on the professional broadcasting standards of the corporation which are used to judge such matters. The film has not changed and those standards have not changed.
Consequently the corporation must determine whether more compelling factors now exist in the realm of public interest. The corporation will give the matter immediate attention at the annual meeting of its board of directors this week and will advise you of its conclusions not later than Thursday, June 25.
As stated already, it is the desire of the corporation to carry out at all times the wishes of parliament.

maintopic: ROOSEVELT-CAMPOBELLO PARK ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION TO ADMINISTER INTERNATIONAL PARK
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-26, respecting the commission established to administer the Roosevelt-Campobello international park.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to move second reading of Bill No. S-26 on the order paper in the name of the Prime Minister respecting the Roosevelt-Campobello international park. As hon. members know, this bill was read for the third time and passed by the Senate on May 28. May I be permitted to give a very brief explanation of the purpose of the bill.
This bill is designed simply to implement the international agreement signed by the President of the United States and by our Prime Minister in Washington on January 22, 1964. The purpose of this agreement was to establish an international park, symbolic of friendship between Canada and the United States, on the property on Campobello island, New Brunswick, which is so clearly identified with the late President Franklin D. Roosevelt. It was here that President Roosevelt was afflicted with the attack of poliomyelitis which impaired his physique from then on but which, however, did nothing to impair the indomitable spirit of courage which was the hallmark of his great service to his own country and to the world in subsequent years.
The agreement signed on January 22 in Washington by the President and the Prime
Roosevelt-Campobello Park Minister concluded months of negotiation between officials of the two governments, in consultation with the province of New Brunswick, where the property is located, regarding the best method for dealing with the generous offer made by the owners of the property, the Hammer brothers, to donate the house and adjacent grounds to the governments of Canada and the United States as a suitable memorial to President Roosevelt and as a symbol of friendship between these two great neighbours.
In May 1963, at the Hyannis Port meeting between the late President Kennedy and Prime Minister Pearson, the Hammer brothers made this offer public and, after communicating with Premier Robichaud, the two heads of government announced their grateful thanks for the offer in principle. The negotiations which followed led to the emergence of the concept of an international commission composed equally of United States and Canadian representatives to administer the proposed park to be established on this site. This concept is embodied in the January 1964 agreement which is annexed to the present bill as the schedule.
At every stage of these negotiations the government of New Brunswick was consulted, and the warm agreement of the New Brunswick authorities to the proposed arrangements was consistently given. I should add that certain aspects of the January agreement involved matters within the provincial jurisdiction of New Brunswick, particularly certain phases of the tax exemptions referred to in article 8 of the agreement. We have been informed that the New Brunswick legislature has already adopted the necessary legislation to implement those aspects of the agreement which fall within the province's jurisdiction.
Meanwhile steady progress is being made in regard to parallel legislation in the United States congress, and all concerned hope that arrangements will be completed in order that the commission may be established and the park opened to tourists as early as possible. Of course, until the necessary legislation has been adopted and the commission formed the title to this property remains with the Hammer family who acquired the property in 1952.
I would like to draw the attention of the house to one or two features of the proposed bill and of the international agreement which is attached as its schedule. It is intended to

Roosevelt-Campobello Park establish an international commission comprising three representatives of each government, together with alternates, who would be responsible for administering the park. It is specifically provided in article 3 of the agreement that one of the Canadian commissioners is to be nominated by the government of New Brunswick and one of the United States commissioners by the government of Maine. Nationals of both countries may be employed on the staff of the commission, and of course the commission has been given all necessary legal powers and capacities to discharge its functions.
I would draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to article 8 of the agreement, which provides that the commission shall be exempt from various federal and local taxes and, as stated, we have been informed that the New Brunswick legislature has already taken action under this article. Regarding admission fees for entrance to the park, the agreement leaves it to the discretion of the commissioners as to whether or not it would be desirable to impose such fees. However, the agreement specifically states that, if the commission decides to impose admission fees, "such fees shall be set at a level which will make the facilities readily available to visitors".
The remaining sections of the agreement and of the implementing legislation are, in my opinion, self explanatory. I should add that in the Senate consideration of this bill the proposed legislation was referred to the Senate committee on external relations where detailed consideration of the bill was given. Officials of various departments appeared as witnesses. In view of this I hope the house will agree that it would not be necessary to refer this bill to our own committee on external affairs.
Therefore I would like to close my remarks with the well-known words of the statesman whom this park is intended to honour. In his first inaugural address on March 4, 1933, President Franklin D. Roosevelt stated, "In the field of world policy I would dedicate this nation to the policy of the good neighbour".

maintopic: ROOSEVELT-CAMPOBELLO PARK ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION TO ADMINISTER INTERNATIONAL PARK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak very briefly in support of Bill S-26 which, when passed, will establish a commission to administer the Roosevelt-Campobello international park. Franklin Delano Roosevelt, who was one of the greatest of the American presidents, came to this part of the country from the time he was one year old until 1921, and

it was on this beautiful little island of Campobello that he contracted poliomyelitis. After his election as president of the United States he returned very infrequently, but he and his family always loved this island and his home on it.
As has been outlined by the Minister of Fisheries, this property was sold by the family in 1952 and for 11 years was in the possession of a private family in the United States, but in 1963 the owners of the property offered it to the governments of Canada and the United States as a memorial to Franklin D. Roosevelt.
I may add that there are other beautiful islands in this part of Canada, in the southwest corner of New Brunswick, such as Grand Manan, Deer island, the Wolves and others where perhaps the kindest people anywhere in Canada can be found. I know that when the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton speaks on this bill he will draw attention to the bridge which was built from Lubec to Campobello, linking the island with the mainland, during the time when he was the distinguished premier of New Brunswick and the right hon. Leader of the Opposition was the prime minister of Canada. That bridge has proven to be of great assistance to the people there, and it will help to make this memorial park one of the greatest tourist attractions in eastern Canada.
I join with the Minister of Fisheries and other hon. members who will be following me in supporting this measure to establish a commission to administer this memorial.

maintopic: ROOSEVELT-CAMPOBELLO PARK ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION TO ADMINISTER INTERNATIONAL PARK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of expressing my great satisfaction that we have this bill before us today, a bill that brings about co-operation between the government of the United States and the government of Canada in contributing to a national shrine to a very great man, a very great friend of Canada and a great leader at a most difficult period in the world's history. I associate myself with everything that has been said by the Minister of Fisheries and the hon. member for York-Sunbury.
We may well express our approval of this measure, because this is one of the few times that the governments of Canada and the United States have jointly purchased property, this time for the express purpose of doing honour to the man whose home was on this island. This park, I am sure, will be a great source of satisfaction to the citizens of both our countries.

I have some personal knowledge of the events leading up to the signing of the agreement. A few years ago the governor of Maine came to Saint John, New Brunswick, to address a meeting, and he and I found ourselves in complete agreement that something should be done in connection with this property. Now, under this agreement, we will have a park established in honour of a very great man, a friend of Campobello island, of New Brunswick, of Canada and of the free world. I am sure the bill will receive the warm approval of every member of the house.
This little island is located in Passama-quoddy bay. It lies south in the province of New Brunswick and at one point is very close to the state of Maine. In fact it is so close that, as was mentioned by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, not too long ago a bridge was constructed with the co-operation of the governments of New Brunswick and Canada and the governments of the state of Maine and the United States of America. This really brings about the possibility of access by tourists to the home of this great man.
Those who have seen the play "Sunrise at Campobello" in one of the New York theatres will remember that the incident when the late president was stricken with poliomyelitis was vividly portrayed; but in spite of never again walking unaided the late president, as we all know, was elected four times to the office of president of the United States. He guided his country through the great depression, and he skilfully and resolutely assisted as much as possible and as quickly and as effectively as possible the struggle of the free world prior to Pearl Harbor and subsequently.
As has been said, the government of New Brunswick is co-operating fully, and I am certain that all Canadians will be pleased, particularly the residents of New Brunswick as well as the people of the state of Maine. The agreement contained in the bill provides that the commission accepts title to the property comprising the Roosevelt home and grounds. The commission is to take the necessary measures to restore the home as nearly as possible to its condition when occupied by President Roosevelt. The commission is to administer as a memorial the Roosevelt Campobello international park. As the minister very properly pointed out, of the six members who will comprise the commission one of the Canadian members will be nominated by the government of New Brunswick and one of the United States members by the government of the state of
Roosevelt-Campobello Park Maine, which seems to me a most excellent idea.
It is very pleasing to me to see that steps are being taken to maintain the summer home of a great president, that steps are being taken to provide that the administrative body shall be composed of representatives from each country, that steps are being taken to do honour to the great president who spent much of his young life and a portion of his mature life in this home, and that steps are being taken so that the public shall have the opportunity of visiting this international shrine. It is most pleasing to know that immediate action is being taken to carry out something that I feel will be in accordance with the desires of all citizens of the United States and Canada. Therefore I have a great degree of pleasure in indicating that I support wholeheartedly the substance of the bill, and I congratulate the minister on presenting it to the house.

maintopic: ROOSEVELT-CAMPOBELLO PARK ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION TO ADMINISTER INTERNATIONAL PARK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we share the general regard for the memory of the late President Roosevelt. One of the paradoxes of his career so far as Canada is concerned is that his popularity in Canada always tended to run ahead of his popularity in the United States. Around 1936, when his career was at its height in political terms, I made my summer living United States tourists, most of them prosperous industrialists or farmers from the corn belt in the middle of the United States. Needless to say they were almost all Republicans, and the comments they used to make about President Roosevelt actually shocked me. I almost thought it was treason that Americans, even Republicans, could think so little of a president.
This came to my mind not long ago during Easter week end when I was in Washington and happened to comment to an old Washingtonian about the fact that there were mobs at the Kennedy grave at Arlington, obviously a shrine, and mobs milling around the Washington monument, the Jefferson memorial and the Lincoln memorial. I said "It is hard to understand why Washington has not created or erected anything in memory of Franklin Roosevelt". I got an answer that might indicate that men who are dead sometimes have to wait for a rewriting of history. This man's answer was "Roosevelt made a lot of mistakes. After all, consider the way he behaved at Yalta. He sold us out to Joe". Then he went on to indicate that the United States has the problem of creeping socialism,

Roosevelt-Campobello Park and that in some ways the late President Roosevelt was responsible for this.
I mention these points because it is so often the case that a great American is looked upon as a greater hero by people outside his country. I think this is especially true of President Roosevelt so far as Canada and Great Britain are concerned. I would hope that the very initiative and part that Canada is playing in this matter will be the beginning of what might be termed a popular return to the real level that we think President Roosevelt should be on in terms of his popularity and his reputation as, in my mind, the greatest of all United States presidents. I know that my colleagues share this very high estimate of the late president.
We think this is an excellent piece of legislation. We do not think Canadians can pay enough tribute to what the late president meant not only to the United States and the world but to his Canadian neighbours.

Mr. Chairman, I know that hon. members wish to take advantage of this motion to discuss immigration matters, during this debate and I wonder if I could make a statement on that subject. I might say right now that my speech will be quite long. However, I am sure that it will enable the committee to understand my point of view on several important aspects of immigration and to clarify misunderstandings, even if certain points should normally be discussed during consideration of my department's estimates.
It goes without saying that I will welcome any question which may be asked here concerning my statement or any other point.
I believe that this budget motion will give me a wonderful opportunity to explain my vews with regard to that important sector of my responsibilities as a minister.
Mr. Chairman, the Department of Citizenship and Immigration has been lately the subject of sharp criticisms from some members of

the House of Commons and other people, with regard to its procedure concerning one aspect of immigration, deportation. As those critics are almost confined entirely to that particular aspect of immigration, they will probably give a wrong impression of the situation.
In order to put the whole question in its true light, to begin with I should like to set out the responsibilities and activities of immigration as a whole, and then to consider the very important matter of deportation, as well as the particular charges levelled against my department in that respect.
The Department of Citizenship and Immigration is entrusted, pursuant to an act of parliament, with two main responsibilities. It rests with it to apply a well-defined immigration policy and for that purpose it must activate the migratory movement, look after the applications for entry, the selection and consideration of a continuous flow of immigrants without sponsors; it must also help them on their arrival, find them a job when necessary, in addition to studying the cases of the large number of immigrants sponsored by relatives.
Immigrants arrive in Canada at an average of 2,000 to 3,000 per week. The second main task of the department is to make easier the controlled movements of non-immigrants in Canada. The latter include tourists, travellers, businessmen, etc. There are over 600,000 such movements per week and this task falls on the department. In view of the large number of people who come to Canada, we really get few complaints about the department's work.
Let us look now at the matter of deportations. They are relatively few. In 1963, for instance, an average of 30 deportation orders a week were issued; in 1964, when the number of immigrants increased considerably, in general the number of deportation orders per week remained practically at the 1963 level. There were a little fewer than 500 deportations between January 1 and April 30. Present criticism against the deportment's procedures is directed at about 20 of those cases. Far be it from me, while comparing that number to the total number of immigrants, to try to underestimate the importance of each person involved. After all, every person is important, and we must see that everyone is treated fairly and equitably. In many cases, an appeal is made to me as minister. I must personally settle some of those cases, and I can assure members of the house that I spend many hours looking into those matters concerning the welfare of the persons concerned. Many individuals are released on a cash or other form of bond, or in some instances on their own recognizance where the special inquiry officer is satisfied that they will respect the conditions of their release and report as required under the law. I appreciate that it must be agonizing for the minister to reflect on some of these human problems. He says that he spent long hours reflecting. I assume Mr. Hooper had lots of time to spend long hours reflecting while the minister was reflecting. We were told that this whole thing blew up because of an administrative breakdown between Toronto and Ottawa. There are members here who seem to be able to travel between Ottawa and Toronto in a very short time any day. The problem is that the officers on the spot are not making decisions and the whole mass of detail has to be referred to the monolith here in Ottawa.
Last week the Ontario minister of reform institution set out a formula-I think this is a very forward step-that he directed to all governors of jails and other institutions within his constitutional jurisdiction. The purpose of the formula is to acquaint people with their rights. The minister, Mr. Grossman, said that because of the constitution he could not interfere with the candidates for jail of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration but at least he could let the department know regularly how long these people had been in these institutions. I hope that the Ontario formula will be followed right across the country so that the ministry of justice and the ministry of immigration in Ottawa will be able to take action when they receive information as to long and inordinate delays.
We were told not too long ago that we would be considering policies to excite the daring. Yet this afternoon we had a long explanation involving a backward step, so far as any such policy is concerned. In my opinion undue detention in jail is an intolerable thing and I say that the minister should be candid enough to admit the error and tell us what procedures he is going to take so that this kind of thing will not happen again.
Before interim supply is granted and we return to the consideration of what I like to term the artificially manufactured issue of the flag I should like to say one or two specific things about some departments of government and the policies they are pursuing. If it is the habit to speak in context or within certain guidelines, I want to do so in the context of the remarkable document published in Forum and also conjointly in Cite Libre in May of this year by a new

Interim Supply
group of seven. Like the group of seven who gave a distinctly Canadian aspect to painting half a century ago, I submit that if we follow some of the policies of today's group of seven we can give a Canadian concept to some of the issues facing us.
It still continues to amaze me that parliament, after it regurgitates the platitudes of debates on the speech from the throne and the cliches of budget debates, hardly ever gets the opportunity to debate on-going policy at all. I should like to refer to a remarkable talk at the Canadian conference on the family a couple of weeks ago by Dean Kaspar Naegle. He is a rather remarkable example that all immigrants are not bad, because this dean of arts of the University of British Columbia spent some time in a prison camp in Canada courtesy of the government during the last war. He reminded those of us who had the privilege of attending the conference of the stricture of T. S. Eliot, "Go, go, go, said the bird: human kind cannot bear very much reality."
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am afraid Canadians cannot bear very much reality, either. All of us here must take some responsibility for the truth of the Eliot adage.
In the manifesto which is entitled, "An Appeal to Realism in Politics", the authors condemn the indifference of the public and private sectors of our society in the face of many problems. The authors say:
We declare our disagreement with most of the panaceas at present in vogue among our politicians.
Canada, today, is a country in search of a purpose. Emphasis on regional interests and the absence of leadership from the central government risk the utter disintegration of the federal state.
In the present context of Canadian politics, it is necessary above all else to reaffirm the importance of the individual-
This is a nice, old fashioned Tory adage.
-without regard to ethnic, geographic or religious accidents. The cornerstone of the social and political order must be the attributes men hold in common, not those that differentiate them. An order of priorities in political and social matters that is founded upon the individual as an individual, is totally incompatible with an order of priorities based upon race, religion or nationality.
I think we should all read this manifesto and take a good deal of it to our hearts. In this context I wish to make an appeal to the minister of citizenship and, I say this modestly, I hope it may help him in some of the unpleasant aspects of his department's policy. I do not hold any brief for Mr. Hooper who recently spent 90 days in the Toronto jail because of what I suggest is an exasperatingly

typical phenomenon-a breakdown in administrative communications. This case need never have reached the stage it did if two basic policies had been followed: One, the local officials in the department should have been able to make decisions, rather than refer every detail to Ottawa; two, counsel should be provided for everyone charged with a breach of the Immigration Act. This latter policy, in my opinion, should be followed in all cases coming under the Criminal Code or federal statutes. This would assure equal justice before the law.
Just the other night I had occasion to speak with a counsel in this city who gave up two weeks of his time to defend a person accused of a very ugly murder. This counsel did this because he had been asked to do so. I believe that in these capital cases the state should look after the counsel fee. This is now the case in the United States. We seem to like copying everything else they do, so it is time we copied this formula.
At the moment the minister is considering what action can be taken against the Greek citizens who admittedly have come to Canada illegally. In some instances they have lived here four or five years, have married and have jobs. If their only offence is illegal entry I submit that in the name of humanity, if for no other reason, the minister should exercise his discretion and permit these people to stay in Canada. I like the type of man who will try to get into this country illegally. I think he has a great future here. It shows a great amount of zeal and daring, qualities which the Liberal government professed to have a year ago but which seem to have been forgotten.
On May 1, 1947, prime minister Mackenzie King said in a debate in the House of Commons that it is not a fundamental human right of any alien to enter Canada, it is a privilege. As a matter of fact, the minister echoed those words today. This classic policy statement was made 17 years ago. I, of course, had not spoken when the minister did, but I think this statement could stand re-examination. By this I mean no criticism of evolving and widening immigration into Canada. I realize that a great educational process is involved and that attitudes must change. However, I am bold enough to believe that we who live in this opulent land in the western world can no longer smugly say that we have a fundamental, God-given right to this land, irrespective of the needs of our brothers in this world. In my opinion, this is the philosophy of 1964 and not-one expounded

17 years ago by Mr. Mackenzie King. The hungry and the wretched in the world are not impressed by Mr. Mackenzie King's narrow strictures. Perhaps while rights are being glibly exhorted in this world, a part of mankind will take up the slogan and adopt it.
Let these people stay in Canada. By their illegal entry, they have already exhibited the qualities of initiative and enterprise which should be useful to all of us. Here I should like to thank the minister for a letter handed to me just before this debate began. For over a year now, the social service council of the Anglican church of Canada has been trying to arrange with the immigration department, as an indication of our concern, the admission of 50 Hong Kong boys to Canada. These boys would be sponsored by and live with Canadian families. They would be given a chance to continue their education, either technical or otherwise. I know the minister views this plan sympathetically, and I am grateful to him for that. He, himself, has been to Hong Kong to check on the administrative procedures there. I earnestly request him to announce soon that his department will agree to this very modest proposal. We had hoped the boys could be in Canada during the early fall of this year so they could continue their education.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal for just a minute-I see it is five o'clock. Will I continue with my observations on interim supply?

subtopic: HONG KONG VETERANS

speakeroldname: Mr. D. W. Groos (Victoria, B.C.) moved:
subtopic: HONG KONG VETERANS
speechtext:
That the standing committee on veterans affairs be empowered to consider the particular circumstances of Hong Kong veterans and to report their opinions and observations as to the special measures that could be undertaken to alleviate the disabilities resulting from the Hong Kong veterans' internment as prisoners of war.
Veterans Affairs
He said: This is not a very complicated measure. I put forward this motion because I am concerned about the lives and the livelihood of upwards of 1,200 Canadian army veterans who served just short of four years as prisoners of war in the Far East.
The men on whose behalf I speak in this house are the Hong Kong veterans and they are the survivors of two Canadian regiments -the Winnipeg Grenadiers and the Royal Rifles of Canada from Quebec city who, together with their brigade headquarters, were sent from Canada to Hong Kong in the closing days of 1941. As we all know, they were subsequently captured and imprisoned and, because this was so, perhaps this is a chapter in Canadian history which some of us would like to put out of our minds. I submit this is something which we cannot do. These men survived almost four years of prison camp life of a type unique in its severity. It was a time of trial for which they were not and could not have been prepared. The figures tell us something of the story. Of a total strength of less than 2,000 men, 228 were killed in the action which preceded the fall of Hong Kong. A further 19 died of wounds resulting from this action and 277 more died in prison camps. In addition, I calculate that another 150, or at least 10 per cent-the figures are not too clear-have since died. I suggest this is a high proportion, considering the age of these men.
I am a veteran and I take the view-I think it is shared by a great many other veterans- that a man has little claim on his country because of what might have happened to him when he was in uniform, but I do earnestly believe that the nation owes at the very least a decent life to veterans who did suffer lasting damage as a result of service in their country's cause. I am sure I can convince members of this house that there is ample evidence to suggest that the Hong Kong veterans, all of whom were prisoners of war, did suffer a great deal during their imprisonment and that they do continue in many ways to feel the effects-the lingering effects-of their imprisonment. Indeed, I believe we owe it to these men to pass the motion now before the house in order that we may establish the facts; in order that we may show these men that we are interested in their difficulties and are prepared to grapple with their problems, and if the existence of those problems is confirmed by the investigation, we must make it clear that we are ready to discharge the nation's responsibility.

Veterans Affairs
The number of prisoners involved in this motion is comparatively small. I am told there are about 1,250 Hong Kong survivors still alive. Most of them are easy to trace, because about 90 per cent of them are in receipt of disability pensions of one kind or another. In spite of their comparatively small numbers there has never been, as far as I can find out, since 1946 a thorough canvass made of these veterans to investigate and analyse their situations, although a sampling was taken in 1950, 14 years ago. I think such an analysis would be revealing. What is disturbing to me is the likelihood that we know little about the after effects and side effects of the type of imprisonment these men endured. For example, there seems to be a disproportionately high number of these men suddenly passing away at an early age without giving any indication that they were ill. The death rate is higher than in the case of a comparable age group. I am advised that one out of every 19 of the Hong Kong veterans who were repatriated is now blind, and that there are many more who have suffered severe eye trouble. It cannot be doubted that this is an unusually high proportion. I think it must follow that the possibility of such things happening has had a disturbing effect on these men. Again, I am told that one out of every five of them is suffering from some degree of hypertension, a dangerous disease of the heart. Although nine out of ten of them are in receipt of disability pensions, as hon. members know, unless a man has been receiving a disability pension to the extent of at least 48 per cent there is no provision for any payment to survivors. I am told that three out of every four of these veterans are in this category, receiving less than 48 per cent disability pensions. So it is no wonder they are worried. I think there are few of us in this house who would not be worried in similar circumstances. And their worry increases each time they hear of another early or unexplained death or disability among their comrades.
If the house, having considered the matter, would agree to pass this motion, I think we shall have taken a step in the direction indicated by the committee on veterans affairs which last year in its report dated December 12, 1963, recommended to the house the following:
In view of the special problems that time and experience have revealed concerning the Hong Kong veterans, this committee urges that a special study and survey be made of their problems and particular disabilities.
[Mr. Groos.l
When this motion is passed I hope the veterans affairs committee will see that such a survey is made. Before entering the house today I was informed that the Canadian pension commission is being authorized to undertake the kind of survey to which I have just referred. I was of course pleased to hear this, since it was in order to encourage such a course that I placed my motion on the order paper last February. However, I do not intend to ask that my motion be withdrawn. I feel that the two proposals-mine, and that of the veterans affairs committee-are complementary and I should like to feel that the members of this house through the committee on veterans affairs would have a hand in directing the course of the survey suggested. If I had my way I would recommend that the survey be not just a sampling, as it was in the past. After all, there are only about 1,200 veterans involved and, as I said before, these men are not hard to find. I think this survey should deal not only with purely medical matters, but that it should extend into the realm of livelihood-the difficulty of maintaining a home, making a living, and so on.
I see that in the past there has been some difference of opinion between the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Hong Kong veterans association with regard to some of the questions which were discussed by the committee last year. When such differences exist, it is, I believe, our duty as members of parliament to find out beyond doubt which side is correct.
The committee last year was presented with a brief by the Hong Kong veterans association which indicated that the very serious lack of food and vitamins, and the general ill treatment suffered by these prisoners produced long hidden side effects which did not disappear when the men affected were outwardly restored to health. These side effects, as I must call them, seem to me to fall into four main categories; there is acute nervousness, heart conditions of one sort or another, trouble with vision, and fatigue. I should point out here, Mr. Speaker, that not all, or for that matter any of these troubles, apply to all Hong Kong veterans; there are some who have been completely rehabilitated and show no evidence of after effects from their wartime experience. But this should not blind us to the unpleasant fact that there is good evidence that an abnormally high number of these veterans are unable to hold on to their jobs in this competitive world. Too many develop serious eye troubles and too many,

as I have said, die suddenly at an early age, leaving behind them wives in their early middle age, and young children.
I was advised only yesterday that in Vancouver, where there are fewer than 200 Hong Kong veterans, three more have died within the past two months, and all three were under the age of 47. These are some of the Canadian youths who volunteered for service in their late teens and early twenties. Mr. Speaker, anyone who like myself, witnessed the return to this country in 1945 of prisoners of war from the Far East will agree with me, I know, that their appearance and their stories of their treatment as prisoners of war will not fade from our memories no matter how long we live.
Before putting forward this motion today I have satisfied myself that we do have a problem here and that it is the responsibility of this house to set matters straight. I have had some difficulty in gathering the facts supporting the motion, but I have had considerable assistance from members of the Hong Kong veterans association, to which I have referred, from the Department of Veterans Affairs and from a group of students at the University of Victoria in my own city of Victoria, B.C., and I would like to thank them for their help. I now seek the approval, the wholehearted approval, of the house for this notice of motion.

subtopic: HONG KONG VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to back this motion of the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) (Mr. Groos). The Hong Kong veterans are a really unique group in one particular aspect, I think. Although we had many prisoners of war in Europe, this group of prisoners was held for over four years under very, very inhuman conditions. I have known some of these veterans myself and I think there is one aspect of their service which I do not want to dwell on too long but which I think is rather unique in this respect. The Canadian soldier generally was well trained, and part of a soldier's training, I think, is to toughen him up so that when he is given the shock of war, the shock of battle, he is mentally prepared for it. A good many of these Hong Kong veterans were shipped over to Hong Kong with very sketchy training indeed, and I would submit that under these circumstances they would go into battle, and into prison, green and scared. I do not mean they would be scared of battle, because Canadian soldiers are magnificent troops, but I think this aspect of being untrained and not pre-
Veterans Affairs
pared for the shock of war had a decided effect in hurting their morale. They felt right from the start that they had not geen given a fair chance to prepare themselves for battle and for prison camp. In addition to that, they were held prisoner in the tropics on the most disgraceful rations you have ever heard of; in fact, some 5 per cent of them have become permanently blind, not to mention the very large number who died under the prison camp conditions. The boys who survived were the toughest of the lot; they were able to stand four and a half years of starvation rations and oriental brutality. As I have said, this bad morale contributed to their mental problem in thinking that they had been somewhat let down by the Canadian people who sent them over there.
Here we have an opportunity to undo, even at this late date, some of the harm that we did to these young men. One of the difficulties, I believe, the pension commission has come up against has always been our very sketchy knowledge of the main disease suffered by these veterans; I think you would call it a disease. They suffered from a vitamin-osis, which I suppose in lay language means being starved to death or to near death. The layman who does not know anything about it says, "Just feed him and he will make a complete recovery"; and some of them have apparently made a near complete recovery. However, I do not think very many of us here could face four and a half years of prison diet and the terrible morale conditions that existed in those camps and expect ever to make a really complete recovery.
These veterans die young. This is one reason-and I am quite sure the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.), will agree with me- why we should give these boys every consideration and should take full advantage of section 70 of the Pension Act, which says that the benefit of the doubt should be given to these veterans in every case. They will not come and ask for help unless they need it. I have known some of these veterans personally. When they came back, although their sight was bad and they could hardly read, they went back to school. I know of one case-I will not mention him by name because he would not want me to do so- where the man went right through university and became a dentist. He was struggling along, often at the bottom of the class, and it was very difficult for him to make his grades. When he joined the army he was top-rate in intelligence and stamina and I would say that if he had gone to university

Veterans Affairs
then he would have stood at the top of his class, instead of being somewhere near the bottom. The only reason he ever did graduate was that he had that same grit and determination which is only too typical of these boys who have tried to rehabilitate themselves under great difficulty after returning home.
The evidence which I have to go on to assess whether or not they are 50 per cent pensioners-and that is what these boys want; they want to be entitled to a 50 per cent pension, particularly because this gives coverage, as was mentioned by the previous speaker, to their widows or orphans-is this: These boys are dying young. Just because we cannot state a special reason for their death and say they died of this or that disease, we know it is because they were prisoners of war in these camps. I know that the pension commission wants to treat all veterans in the same way, and some objection has been taken to calling them Hong Kong veterans. It has been suggested that perhaps they are asking for something special. I claim they are not asking for anything which we would not give to any other veteran under the same circumstances, because one and all they were prisoners for the same length of time. I think it is quite safe to group them together in this way and say that any man who spent four and half years in a Japanese prison camp is only 50 per cent effective physically.
I do not believe that any one of these men could go, for instance, to a lumber camp, work alongside other men who had not been through this struggle and be, say, any more than half as good. The whole principle behind giving pensions to soldiers has been based on their ability to earn their living with their own hands. We have never suggested that we should compensate a soldier for the loss of a great career on the stage, a career in law or medicine, or something like that. We have always said that we would compensate them in relation to helping, say, their fathers on the farm. If a man is able only to take care of the horses or to saw boards in the bush, we would give him 50 per cent pension. The fact that he is still six feet tall is irrelevant.
From personal knowledge of these men who have come out of these camps, having worked alongside them, I submit that they are no more than 50 per cent physically effective. If they were to come forward, either individually or as a group, and were able to say that there is plenty of evidence to show that

Hong Kong veterans are no more than 50 per cent effective in terms of physical ability, then I do not think there is any argument against this proposal. The main evidence before the pension commission has always been that of Dr. Crawford, who was in one of these camps himself. He personally is a magnificent specimen of physique. He has tremendous mental stability, which is doubtless shown by the fact that he is still able to carry a tremendous burden as medical adviser to the department. But I do not think we could use a man like Dr. Crawford as the criterion. Our job here is to deal with average men. We do not look for physical or mental giants when assessing the ability of the average soldier to stand up to this terrible ordeal. Therefore I think we must go further afield than a case like Dr. Crawford-and I am not being sarcastic in saying that. He is the hero type. He has been a hero in the way he has rehabilitated himself, and the contribution he has made since the war. I am not trying to cut these other fellows down, but the average man cannot be expected to put up with what these fellows put up with and come through with flying colours.
I think there is evidence which could be produced when this commission or board is set up. I think we could go to the Japanese themselves, now that the war is over. I am sure the Japanese must have had thousands and thousands of prisoners from other nations, and even their own, who were treated in the same way. Perhaps there is medical evidence to be found in Japan of this same disease from which our Hong Kong veterans are suffering.
I am very pleased to hear that some notice has been taken of our plea in the veterans affairs committee to set up such a commission, as asked for by the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.); and I am sure there are other hon. members who would like to say a few words about this. We certainly do not want to talk this measure out. If it is only a question of spending a little money to make a proper survey, I would certainly recommend such expenditure. I would go further and say that if we are to take section 70 of the Pension Act at face value it would be no crime against the Canadian taxpayer to give the benefit of the doubt to any of these men who spent four and a half years in a Japanese prison camp, and to give them an entitlement to at least a 50 per cent pension, thereby protecting the wives who have stood by them all these years, and the children who make

it difficult to get along with a reduced scale of living. Because I submit these boys are just not capable of earning a living 100 per cent with their hands.

subtopic: HONG KONG VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to give support to this motion which has been proposed by the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) (Mr. Groos). I believe it to be a very worthy matter deserving of the support of every hon member in this house. I personally know many of the veterans who came out of the Hong Kong affair, and I know something of the problems faced by practically all of these men. Likewise it has been my privilege to visit the cemetery in Hong Kong and to thoroughly explore the actual locations where the fighting took place, where many of our Canadian boys gave their lives and where many of those who are still with us were taken prisoner. I have seen some of the projects they were forced to work at through compulsory labour, before many of them were moved to Japan and other parts. In fact, when one lands on the runway at Hong Kong airport today he is landing on top of rocks carried there by the hands of many of these Hong Kong veterans during their period of compulsory labour while detailed in Hong Kong prison camps.
All of the Hong Kong veterans at the time of their return from imprisonment showed the adverse effects of their experiences in varying degrees. The treatment and care which has been given them subsequently has in many cases rebuilt physical bodies, and restored health at least in some measure. But one of the most difficult aspects of being able to judge just how much disability is involved as far as these veterans are concerned revolves around the fact that many of their disabilities cannot be measured as the normal disability from the effects of war is measured. It is comparatively easy to categorize a man's pension rights from the loss of a limb or other physical disability, but in the conditions under which these men lived for four and a half years they often broke down psychologically and physically in a way upon which it is very difficult today to place a measurement. Therefore it is my opinion that every one of the Hong Kong veterans is deserving of some kind of pension remuneration, and we should be thinking about this while we still have a sizeable number of them with us. Because they are rapidly leaving the scene.
Veterans Affairs
I have before me a statement which was part of a brief presented to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet) by the Hong Kong veterans association. It concerns the increase of pension and the entitlement to medical care for these veterans. One statement in the brief impressed itself upon me and I would like to share it with others. It is as follows:
The psychological stresses to which Hong Kong veterans were subjected during their period of imprisonment were severe and long continued. Four years of rough treatment, beatings and constant threat of torture in many forms, stress of undernourishment, inadequate clothing along with forced labour under intolerable conditions, have left hidden personality scars which continue to lower these veterans' ability to adjust into normal civilian life. Even cursory observation of many of these veterans today will verify the permanent damage that was suffered under deplorable conditions experienced by no other prisoner of war.
This brings me to the point that it is not only the physical problem which these veterans face but also the psychological and mental problems, which represent even a greater difficulty sometimes than physical incapacity. They are not requesting any special treatment. If there is any group of veterans deserving of our consideration, I believe it is this group. What they have asked for is reasonable and should be considered. There would be no better way for these things to be brought into public focus than to permit the veterans affairs committee to undertake a study of not just a few but, as has been mentioned by the mover of the motion, of as many as possible,-in fact of all the veterans, in order to determine accurately what our responsibilities are to them.
I should like to outline some of the things these veterans are seeking. First, they are asking that present pensions be reviewed for all Hong Kong veterans. They are also asking that a revival of the survey started in 1950 be undertaken, and that there should be a yearly regular check-up of every individual. They are asking for the supplying of eyeglasses, and dental care without question. They ask for a study of the effects of avitaminosis and other diseases which they developed as a result of dietary deficiency. They ask for a study of the effects of beri-beri, pelagra and dysentery to establish without question the connection between them and their present disabilities such as optic atrophy, cardiac deficiencies, nerve destruction, stomach conditions, etc.
They are also asking an award of a minimum 50 per cent of pension for residual effects of avitaminosis to every ex-Japanese

Veterans Affairs
prisoner of war. The previous speaker mentioned that it was not fair to condemn them for seeking special privileges over and above other prisoners of war. It would be very easy to categorize all prisoners of war in the same class, prisoners who went through similar situations whether out of Hong Kong or some other place.
These men ask that all Hong Kong prisoners of war be given complete entitlement to normal pension provisions. I believe these are very reasonable requests. Therefore on behalf of this party I give our complete support to the motion and hope it will be passed by the house so that the veterans affairs committee may make recommendations covering these prisoners. In fact, I find it difficult to understand why this problem has been passed over for so many years. Therefore I would urge the house to permit the passage of this motion today.

subtopic: HONG KONG VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the motion presented by the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) (Mr. Groos). The hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg) quite correctly referred to the fact that these troops from the Royal Rifles and the Winnipeg Grenadiers went to Hong Kong in 1941 without top level training. There is something else that should be pointed out, Mr. Speaker, and it is that the Hong Kong contingent was entirely without any mechanical transport.
The majority sailed on the Amatea, a British naval transport, on October 26, 1941. Originally it was intended that the force be supplied with 212 motor vehicles composed of 45 motorcycles, 6 Ford cars, 57 universal carriers, 63 15-cwt. trucks, 2 15-cwt. water tanks and 39 3-ton trucks, but due to various administrative difficulties none of these vehicles arrived at the docks in Vancouver until October 27 and 28 when the Amatea had already sailed, along with H.M.C.S. Prince Rupert, an escort vessel, which carried four officers and 105 other personnel.
What happened then is history. All the vehicles were loaded on the Don Jose, an American freighter, which set sail on November 4, 1941, bound for Hong Kong, but was re-routed to Manila and authority was subsequently given by the Canadian authorities to have these vehicles used by American troops. It may seem, Mr. Speaker, that I am digressing a little, but I think there is a lesson to be learned from this, and I am happy to see that in the white paper on defence, and in the all party special committee on defence,

matters like this are under consideration, so that we shall have transport available for highly mobile forces in future.
The casualties suffered by the Canadians in Hong Kong, due to fighting, and later malnutrition and the cruel treatment they received, were very heavy indeed. As a matter of fact, the losses from December 8, 1941 until December 25, 1941 were very heavy. At brigade headquarters five officers and 16 other ranks were either killed or died of their wounds, while in the Royal Rifles seven officers and 123 other ranks were killed or died of their wounds. Fatal casualties among the Winnipeg Grenadiers totalled 11 officers and 128 other ranks. But this is only part of the story.
They then suffered further harrowing experiences. Until 1943 they were all kept in prisoner of war camps at Hong Kong, and as a result of the deplorable conditions there four more officers and 124 other ranks died. It is of interest, as was pointed out by Colonel Stacey, in his official Canadian war history, that the losses would have been much more severe except for a very ironical situation. There was an outbreak of diphtheria in the camps and the Canadian prisoners were refused medical supplies to treat the disease. As a result of that they in turn infected some of the Japanese guards with diphtheria, and the Canadians were then taken off their heavy work details and placed in isolation. Perhaps, inadvertently, more lives were saved as a result of that outbreak than would otherwise have been the case.
In January, 1943, 1,183 other ranks together with one officer, significantly a Captain J. A. G. Reid, of the Royal Canadian Army Medical Corps, were taken to Japan and were forced to work in various industries, chiefly mining. Again the conditions were extremely bad and this can be shown as evidenced by the fact that here 136 more men died.
I was very happy, Mr. Speaker, to hear my hon. friend from Victoria (B.C.) announce that the Canadian pension commission is now prepared to launch an investigation into the status of these Hong Kong veterans. I expect this investigation is designed to produce information about the Hong Kong veterans and to give some indication of points which will require further and more detailed investigation. I have asked for other information, and I would like to refer to an article concerning this whole matter, which appeared in the Victoria Daily Times of June 13, 1964. It is stated there that the death rate among

these men, referring to the Hong Kong veterans, is 27 per cent. I have asked for information on this point, and I imagine that there probably must be a typographical error because up to the end of 1963, 108 of the over 1,400 men who were repatriated to Canada after the war had died. This is a death rate of approximately 7.7 per cent. Certainly we are not happy about this at all and we must look into the matter further, but the figure is not 27 per cent as reported in the Victoria Times. I think this bears correcting.
There is no question in my mind that these men suffered more and for a greater length of time than the ordinary, if I may use that word, prisoner of war in other parts of the world. There is no question in my mind that they are deserving, not of special treatment but of treatment which will assure them justice.

Veterans Affairs
had been referred not only to myself but to other members, having in mind the possible influence we might have with regard to the determination of the course to be followed by the department or by the government.
I make the same plea to the present government as I made to the former government. The hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) has made it very clear, and other members have supported him, that these veterans require something a little different and a little more specialized in the way of treatment than other veterans. However, I should like to see included in this motion all members of the forces who were interned in prison camps.
I say that because of cases with which I am well acquainted personally. In the course of the next two or three days a veteran with whom I had the privilege of serving will be coming to Ottawa to determine if any assistance from the government is available to him because of the special circumstances mentioned by one member who participated in the debate. This problem is a continuing one. As my colleague who participated in the debate has mentioned, these people sometimes will not come forward themselves until it is too late. Sometimes it is the case that they have made no representations at all to the Department of Veterans Affairs since 1945 and therefore it is a very easy thing for the departmental officials to say that their condition is in no way related to their wartime experiences.
I think of names such as Bill Warren. I do not recall his home town but he was in the camp I was in, and I know this man has a justifiable case. His case has been before the pension commission on several occasions but now the door is completely closed. There is a widow in the province of Manitoba with a family of young children, and I know the difficulty this veteran had when he was in the camp. It was precisely his experiences there which caused his death. The same is true of my colleague and friend, Danny Evans of Toronto. There is also the case of a young widow of a year and a half ago in the city of Hamilton. Now we have this chap coming to Ottawa in the course of the next few days.
In each and every case their own doctors have said that their condition is attributable to the severe experiences they had in the prison camps. Some of us who were there may not show signs of what had to be endured. As a matter of fact, I recall that when I returned home I weighed approximately 128 pounds. I wish I were a little closer to that mark today, but that is beside the point. Some

people have not been as fortunate as some of us. There are quite a number of members in the house who have had these experiences and can well appreciate the sensible views that have been put forward today.
I appreciated the eight points that were set down by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson). There is not one of them that would not apply to every colleague of mine who was in southeastern Germany. Perhaps our treatment was not as rough as that given out to the Hong Kong veterans. I qualified my remarks at the beginning with that statement. However, I wish the hon. member had included these people in his motion because the cases I have mentioned all seem to me to have a common denominator, and that is the life they endured as members of the services and the experiences they had to go through.
I could mention to the house specific instances. I can remember one day in particular when there was a great escape. The German authorities sent their storm troopers into the camp, about 300 of them. They were lined up across the front and down one side with their tommy guns at the fire. When they did not get the kind of co-operation they wanted, some officer in the wehrmacht blew his top and all of these guards started blasting down in between the camp, through the barracks and so on. This lasted for a period of two days. Throughout the whole night, people had to stand out on the parade ground, make fires, and so on. Though this is only one incident, but such experiences as these had a reaction on the people and left a mark on them. In addition, there were deprivations, diet and so on. There should be a recognition of the things mentioned specifically by the hon. member for Red Deer, as well as those referred to by the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.)
I should like very much to have this motion include all those who have been in prisoner of war camps. Dr. Crawford in the department knows that I brought this matter to the attention of the committee many years ago. He said that it was difficult to get any statistics covering these people because of the situation which exists in Canada. I did not know until a short time ago that this subject would be discussed today or I would have endeavoured to produce some of the information that was given to the committee at that time. I assure you that the statistics that have been given to us here apply equally right across the board to the people who have had these experiences. I will be very

satisfied if during the course of this particular study it is borne in mind that the people I have mentioned have particular rights. I have only referred to these cases from memory, but all cases of a similar type should be given special consideration. If this is done I will consider it a wonderful effort on the part of the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.), the committee on veterans affairs and the Canadian parliament. I am grateful to the hon. member for bringing this forward now and I am pleased to support the terms of the motion.

As we have wide rules of relevancy in this debate I wish to say a word or two now about the question of Canadian unity.
I have much sympathy with the aspirations of Quebec and its so-called quiet revolution. I think we in the rest of Canada must understand that this revolution is directed as much against the past in Quebec as it is against the rest of Canada. I think we must remind ourselves of the French fact in Canada and of the perfectly natural desire for this great culture to preserve its language in a changing country and a changing world. Having said that, I say with great respect to my Quebec confreres. Do not let the quiet revolution become so inward looking that its aspirations make Quebec a narrow, insulated community in Canada, in North America and in the world. If this is the consequence of the present movement, it is a movement in defiance of man's progress in the 20th century. Nationalism in the restrictive sense became outmoded when bombs fell on Hiroshima. Turn outward, so that Canada and the world may share the fruits of your culture and your learning. As the manifesto which I discussed earlier this evening puts it:
The future of a language depends upon the dynamism of those who speak it. ..To use nationalism as a yardstick deciding policies is both sterile and retrograde. Overflowing nationalism distorts one's vision of reality, prevents one from seeing problems in their true perspective, falsifies solutions and constitutes a classic diversionary tactic for politicians caught by facts.
In saying this I do not speak only to Quebec. I speak about all those manifestations of nationalism current in our land. Little Englanders must not be transplanted here as little Canadians. To quote again from the manifesto:
The most valid trends today are toward more enlightened humanism, toward various forms of political, social and economic universalism. Canada is a reproduction on a smaller and simpler scale of this universal phenomenon. The challenge is for a number of ethnic groups to live together.

It is a modern challenge, meaningful and indicative of what can be expected from man.
I have no trained and sophisticated mechanism which can tell me what is in the minds of the people of Canada, but I have a hunch that we parliamentarians would be surprised to learn that the truth of some, at least, of what I say, is well understood by many people all across this land. I suggest-and here again I adopt the words of the manifesto-that to confess one's inability to make confederation work is, at this stage of history, to admit one's unworthiness to contribute to the universal order.
I cannot think that Canadians of whatever origin-as if origin mattered-are going to turn our backs on what Sir Ernest Barker calls, in an important book, "The Tradition of Civility". Canada is indeed a small reproduction of that part of the world which established for men everywhere the great salutary rules which are part of what Walter Lippmann terms the "public philosophy"-the "public philosophy" from which springs freedom of religion, of thought and of speech. Some of this public philosophy is embedded in bills of rights, other parts in jurisprudence and others in constitutions.
Sir Ernest Barker puts it this way:
The rational faculty of man was conceived asr producing a common conception of law and order which possessed a universal validity-
I am suggesting that it is our duty and responsibility to make sure it does not wither and die from neglect. It is a greater responsibility than a design for a flag or a revision of a constitution. It is of more importance than preserving an international boundary or a parochial pattern. The list of Canada's priorities-and this is what I believe we are considering-is too long for me to capitulate in any detail tonight. But it includes the fight against poverty-and may I remind hon. members that dramatic schemes to clear city slums leave untouched that wasteland of rural poverty which can be seen in too many parts of my own province and, I suppose, in others. It includes unemployment, particularly regional unemployment, and the parallel problem of the inequitable distribution of wealth and income. It includes the pollution of our streams and rivers and the erosion of our soil; it includes ruthless exploitation of some of our heritage; it includes the monotonous pap of some of our radio and television programs, which seem to be based on a denominator which is often subterranean. It includes an antiquated penal system where, too often,

punishment is substituted for rehabilitation; crowded hospitals and a lack of decent provisions for proud and honest men to settle their doctors bills. It includes people who will not recognize the French cultural fact, and the reasonable wish on the part of this cofounding race to maintain its tongue and enlarge its share of the development of the whole of Canada. It includes, unfortunately, a still pitifully inadequate foreign aid program and, with great respect to the minister of citizenship, a much too restrictive formula for immigration into this country.
Mr. Chairman, I said we had a responsibility, and I think we do. We have a responsibility to public opinion, and I am going to suggest that public opinion is not just an unworked lump of dough; it needs yeast to make it work-and I suggest that it is our responsibility to be that yeast. Walter Lippman reminds us that, "The naively democratic theory was that out of the mass of the voters there arose a cloud of wills which ascended to heaven, condensed into a thunderbolt, and then smote the people". We as political people-and I am proud of that adjective -know that this is not so.
James Reston wrote in a column in the New York Times on March 28:
We must not demand the serenity of faith without the agony, victory without the struggle, solvency without the taxes, leadership without the .criticism, peace without sacrifice, and salvation without conviction.
