One of the first points I would like to bring up is one I have repeatedly mentioned in the house. Unfortunately, we did not see any improvement in this field. I am speaking of the behaviour of employees in the Quebec office of the income tax department.
After my having complained time and again in the house, the Minister of National Revenue suggested that I should submit to him the cases I might have so that he could examine them and see what is wrong with the office of his department at Quebec. During the past two months-and the minister will be able to -confirm this-I have sent him at least three score letters from people in the county of Lapointe who were dissatisfied with the decisions of the inspectors at the Quebec office.
Mr. Chairman, I hardly know whether the minister looked into those cases, or whether
Interim Supply
he had some inquiry made to see what was happening in his department, but there is one thing I know, which is that we always get the same routine: the inspectors of the Quebec office of the Department of National Revenue behave like dictators and tyrants, depriving people of their savings.
I have received some letters signed by the Minister of National Revenue to the effect that his inspectors in Quebec had consulted the parish priests in their rectories. Now, parish priests from the riding of Lapointe have sent me sworn statements to the effect that no inspector from the Quebec office has ever come to their rectory to secure information in that connection. Mr. Chairman, I will send those sworn statements to the Minister of National Revenue and I think it will then be time for him to open his eyes and realize that officials of his department in Quebec are purely and simply robbing the people by reducing their deductions for charitable donations, though there are receipts signed by parish priests who swear that the inspectors of the Department of National Revenue never came to see them.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, that is serious, because we are told that enquiries are made when there are none. What happens is merely that an official stays at his desk in his office where he makes an arbitrary decision to rob the people of their income.
Those dictators of the income tax office make a great show to try to get promotions, and when they can make the Department of National Revenue save a few dollars, such promotions are given to them under the pretext that they are good servants.

Mr. Mcllraith's signature, i.e. the signature of the Minister of National Revenue-to say that, on his instructions, his officers went to a rectory to get some information with re-

gard to a particular case, and the priest, in his turn, sends me a letter under oath certified by a notary, to the effect that nobody from the national revenue office ever appeared at his rectory to ask for information on this matter.

Now, Mr. Chairman, let us take another department. I see that the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) are not present, but since we are in the farming season, I should like to make a request to the government, through the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Forestry, whichever department is concerned.
We realize that in the province of Quebec there are not enough farm credit advisers. There are many applications made by farmers for loans. Unfortunately, there are not enough farm credit advisers or inspectors to go and make inquiries at the place of all the farmers who make applications, so that the granting of loans is delayed and, of course, the farmers are delayed in their seeding or in their crops, and it is Quebec agriculture that suffers.
I think that in a province such as Saskatchewan, with 15 or 16 counties, there are 37 inspectors or supervisors of farm credit. In the province of Quebec, with a population seven times larger, there are hardly 16 of them.
1 think that all members of the house will recognize that there is discrimination there. I am in favour of those 37 advisers or supervisors of farm credit in Saskatchewan, and if they want more, I am not against it. But when there are not enough in the province of Quebec to meet the needs, I cannot help but protest.
That leads me to say that there is something wrong in our system. I think that there

is overlapping by the federal government and the provincial government in too many fields.
There is some in agriculture. When something has to be settled in agriculture, steps must be taken with the provincial government and then with the federal government. It takes time to convince the provincial government and then it takes time to convince the federal government, and it takes even more time to convince both of them together. When some ARDA project has to be carried out, it has to go through the provincial government and the provincial government must go to the federal government and then it comes back to the provincial government, so that the delays are three times longer than if there were only one government to look after that. The same thing happens with respect to winter works. The municipality applies to the provincial government; the matter has to be referred to the federal government, then it is returned to the provincial government, and, finally, it comes back to the municipality.
This implies a loss of time, some delays causing trouble for interested parties and bodies. As regards winter works ARDA and farm credit, pension plans and any other field, we see two governments interfering with each other; each has a decision to make, each one has its own legislation, its rules and regulations. In such circumstances, delays are bound to occur and everything is being neglected.
This leads us to conclude that an end should be put to those programs where two governments must be consulted and where two governments must legislate before results are obtained. In my opinion, the federal government should withdraw purely and simply and leave sources of income to the provinces in order that they may be in a position to deal alone and by themselves with such problems, and that these be settled sooner and to everybody's satisfaction.
It is obvious that if the council of ministers, before reaching a decision, was obliged to consult the cabinet or the council of ministers in Mexico, our country would suffer because it would take from now to doomsday to get action. That is exactly what occurs in every field with the joint plans.
There are too many governments, too many different things, too many levels of government, so that everything is delayed and everything is bungled. This leads us to an inevitable conclusion; the federal government must withdraw as soon as possible from joint plans
Interim Supply
to allow the provincial governments to legislate in the fields these plans cover at present.
What creates most problems nowadays in Canada for the federal government, for provincial and municipal governments, and also for individuals, is that the Canadian citizens, in the economic field, do not think as Canadian citizens but as a colonized people subject to other countries.
I read recently, and this is one of the things which disgusts me the most in our country's administration, that in our international trade, we had, during the last three months, in our goods account only, a surplus of $47 or $48 million. On the other hand, we notice that we have a deficit of approximately $375 million concerning the outflow of money.
Why all this? Because each year there is $1,200 million-this is a huge amount, Mr. Chairman-which is paid by Canada to other countries for interest, dividends or benefits to foreign companies who are developing natural resources of our country.
I came back yesterday, having held several meetings in the Chicoutimi county, in an area where we find a good number of lumbermen. Now, these men are cutting wood for $5 a cord, are paying their room and board in the forest, and their power saw at the end of the season; they come back more indebted, having barely enough to live on, while foreigners, who do not even come and fell a single tree in our forests, who do not even know what our trees look like, collect the profits and lead an easy life in other countries thanks to the profits due to the labour of our people.
Mr. Chairman, I say that the Canadian people today, are an economically colonized people who only work for wages, while the benefits, dividends and interests are going at a rate of $1,200 million a year to foreign countries, to make their capitalists richer.
If that problem were solved, if there were organized in this country a system whereby we would remain masters of our natural resources, of our industry, of our forests and waters, we could keep the benefits, dividends and interests for ourselves and each year our country would be $1,200 million richer.
Imagine what we could do with all that money. We could build schools, colleges, universities, pay our professors and build hospitals.
And in the province of Quebec, persons who are ill have to wait 15 days, three weeks or a month to be admitted to hospital, because there is a shortage of hospital beds.

Interim Supply
Mr. Chairman, with $1,200 million we could build hospitals, roads and bridges, we could develop our industry and increase family allowances. Can you imagine what would be within our reach if dividends earned in Canada remained in our province? Unfortunately those profits go elsewhere.
Mr. Chairman, that is precisely what is wrong with this country; it has no control over its capital, and its credit and its citizens remain small wage earners while foreigners make all the profits. I have nothing against their getting the profits in their own country but I object to their laying their hands on the profits in Canada just because they can afford to provide the required capital and we cannot.
When we settle that problem a lot of others will be solved at the same time. When we can create our own credit and keep our own profits instead of letting them fall into foreign hands, then quite a few problems will have been solved.
Those are the few comments I wanted to make.
I also wanted to refer briefly to a rather typical example of patronage. We have just found out that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has seen fit to hire, at $7,500 a year, an individual who works for him in his riding of Matapedia-Matane. I am wondering whether there are a great many immigrants in that constituency or if the man's job is to look after patronage or to prepare elections on behalf of the minister.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege.
The hon. member said that I hired an official and suggests that he is looking after patronage in my constituency. I will point out to the hon. member that this official belongs to my Ottawa office and that he has always been on my staff, but it is true that he has been performing certain duties, which I am unable to do as Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in my own constituency.

He was exclusively appointed in Ottawa and in my constituency, where I cannot deal with the correspondence of every case submitted to me as a minister or a member of parliament.

I feel that the minister did not give us enough information, but it is easy to see what it means.

In my riding, when constituents complain that the bandits of the income tax division have cut down their receipts for charitable donations, I am the one who has to settle the matter. It is never done by an official, because the department does not want the matter to be settled. But when this happens in the riding of Matapedia-Matane, the minister has an official deal with the matter on his behalf.
The same applies when problems relating to farm credit and unemployment insurance have to be settled. We have to write to the Quebec office, but inspectors are too few and it takes time to settle the matter. As for the minister, he is lucky, because he has someone in this riding to look after farm credit and unemployment insurance matters, and when a tax problem arises and the bandits of the income tax division do not want it to be settled-

Mr. Chairman, when the hon. member uses the word "bandit" to designate officials of the Department of National Revenue, he goes far beyond the parliamentary terms used in the house, and I would therefore ask him to withdraw his words.

I do not know whether the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) was here a while ago when I mentioned tioned that inspectors stated that they made inquiries in rectories and that parish priests claim that they have not received the visit of an inspector. Then, when I see that inspections are being made directly in the inspector's office, and I can prove it, I find that we are using the term very loosely. I do not know how the hon. member calls that, but I think the term is quite proper and I will not withdraw my words. I will only withdraw them if it is proven that I am wrong. But, it will not be proven, not with all the facts I now have. The term is sufficiently loose not to go beyond what I have in mind.
If the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration wants to present in his constituency-

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has asked the member who insulted the federal officials to withdraw. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, to make a ruling on that question of privilege.

Maybe these problems do not occur in the riding of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard). It is also possible that if he would visit his electors a little more often, he might realize that this problem is there. As for us, we want to serve the interests of our electors, and that is normal. We object because we know that in

his riding the situation is similar and I know that his electors complain, the same as in other ridings; that is why I am surprised to see his attitude, to see him rise and make-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member for Lapointe, in the remarks he is now giving, is making them directly against officials of the department. If he has any criticism of the department to make it would be more in order if he made it to the minister.
The civil servants are not here to defend themselves. You are being cowardly.

It is obvious that I am making remarks and that I cannot treat the minister like that, since he does not take such action himself; his senior officials do it for him, because if he had to deal with all the cases, he would really have too much to do. On the other hand, his responsibility is to see that his officials do not behave like they do and, if they behave badly, it is his responsibility to set his department in order.
As I was saying, I think the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane is very fortunate to have been able to hire a civil servant solely to look after such problems. They take up a lot of our time, because our electors feel that things are going badly in all those fields, income tax, farm credit, unemployment insurance. As far as the minister is concerned, he has somebody to look after all those things. But we have no one. The minister is assisted by officials to do his research work in the house. He even employed some one to go and see his electors and calm them. As far as we are concerned, we try to settle those things directly with the department without any patronage in the riding. The minister should avoid patronage when he employs someone to look after all his little worries and try to quiet the discontented ones and make friends with them.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege.
I do not think that members can use the word "patronage" to describe the services rendered by someone to all the electors of a riding who have needs or requests to be made known to the government.
Therefore, I ask the hon. member to withdraw the word "patronage" to describe the services rendered by a member of parliament, by a minister or by one of his officials 20220-291

who deals with the correspondence and tells the minister about the goings on in his county.
I do not think that we can use the word "patronage" to describe such activities and, therefore, I ask him to withdraw that word.

Mr. Chairman, with respect to the question of privilege, let the minister see to it that there is an individual like that in every riding in Canada. Then, when there is one everywhere, we will not hear the ministers' say: It is because they want to arrange their little schemes in their ridings.
We do not have such employees; we have to spend our week ends visiting the homes of those farmers, seeing electors, but we see them, we talk with them, we know them; it is not officials who do our job for us because we go and see our own people; this is much more satisfactory, because when we come back to the house, we can say that as representatives we talk knowingly because we visited them, we saw them, we met them and we discussed their problems with them.
Mr. Chairman, the minister did not tell us exactly what were the duties of this Mr. Cote who is paid $7,500 per year to work for the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, because I imagine that the minister must have many immigrants in his riding of Matapedia-Matane. Can he tell us what are his duties and what cases he tried to solve down there? Perhaps the minister could give us more details and inform us of the duties of this official, and then perhaps patronage would not be mentioned so much.
Mr. Chairman, I wanted, while we are discussing interim supply, to avail myself of the opportunity of expressing some views, because it is not always possible to vent our thoughts on various issues.
I wanted to deal with farm credit, for while I think that inspectors are doing a good job, there are too few of them. I would ask the government to increase the number of supervisors and farm credit advisers, more particularly in the province of Quebec, to answer the need.
I also would ask the Minister of National Revenue to put some order into his department, more particularly in the Quebec office.
And, if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) were able to give this country a financial system enabling Canadians to develop their own industries, natural resources and trade, by their own means, instead of having them developed by foreigners, then

Interim Supply
we would keep our profits at home, and develop Quebec better than we do now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in the early part of his remarks, the hon. member for Lapointe dealt at some length with the Department of National Revenue, of which department I am the acting minister. In the course of his remarks he referred to the civil servants of the department as tyrants, dictators, robbers and several other terms of that nature.
He does not know any other language.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I merely want to point out that it is quite contrary to the usage and practice of the house to refer to civil servants in that way, for the rather obvious reason that it has always been thought to be improper to refer to persons who are unable to defend themselves. It is improper to take advantage of the privilege of the house-where they cannot reply-to use language in reference to them that could not be used outside the house without incurring the responsibility consequent on such actions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Spank him some more.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think the abuse of the correct practice and procedures of the house will be apparent to anyone who gives the matter any thought. Having objected to this wholly improper practice, I think I can leave the matter there for the moment.
The hon. member's other remarks concerning the department had to do with claims for charitable donations by taxpayers in certain parts of his constituency, those claims in a large number of cases having run to 10 per cent of income. There has been some question whether or not these claims for charitable donations were made due to a misunderstanding of the law or whether in fact the amount of money claimed as having been donated to charities was actually so donated.
As I understand the duty of the minister, it is to see that the act is administered fairly. That implies that each taxpayer is treated fairly under the provisions of the act-
They are not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
-as the law requires that they shall be treated. Under our modern system, practically every citizen is a taxpayer and it is important that the taxpayer who pays his taxes should know and be able to feel that all other taxpayers are being

required to pay their taxes on an equal footing under the law. If that has meant the investigation of certain individual cases, surely that is the necessary and proper thing to do.
Each case the hon. member has referred to me has been checked or is being checked. When he says that he sends a letter a day about some particular taxpayer, I can only tell the committee that he is being quite accurate: In fact, I thought it was more than a letter a day. In any event, whatever the number, these cases are checked in each instance to find out if these people have been treated fairly and in accordance with the law. As best that can be done, it is being done.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As I have indicated, in some areas there is a misunderstanding as to what the law is.
The misunderstanding is in the department.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The fact is that actual donations up to a maximum of 10 per cent of income are what are allowed, but there seems to be an impression in some areas of the hon. member's constituency that there is an allowance of 10 per cent of income for such donations, which is quite a different thing. I assure the hon. member that as long as I have the responsibility as acting minister for this particular portfolio, the cases he refers will be looked into and dealt with. If he has any particular complaints and can substantiate them, I will be very glad to receive the information and, they will be looked into.
The hon. member also referred to the matter of affidavits. Offhand I have no recollection of receiving any such affidavits, but if there are any such affidavits that appear to be in conflict with our information or to add information that has a bearing on a particular case, I certainly will be glad to see that they are properly examined to make sure that the law is administered with absolute fairness. This is the only way that a system as all-embracing as our present taxation system can be administered.
May I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: By all means.

Is it not a fact that in many of the cases I have sent the minister the people were claiming only 6 or 7 per cent of

their net income, and not 10 per cent as the minister mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I would not agree that is so. The point is that they are only entitled to claim what they actually gave to charities. That is the point. They are only entitled to claim what they actually gave up to a maximum of 10 per cent of their income.

Mr. Chairman, if the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration were a philosopher instead of an economist I suppose he could console himself with the fact that the criticism he and his department have received in the last month or so is the same as the criticism levelled at nearly every minister of citizenship and immigration for the last 15 or more years. I think the only person who escaped that criticism was the minister who preceded him, and I suppose he only escaped it because he did not remain in the department long enough for some of us to get at him.
I think that anyone who wants to be realistic will realize that the minister is not entirely responsible for the difficulties in which he finds himself, but rather it is the Immigration Act, the regulations drafted for the administration of the act and the administration itself which has become so involved and so obviously discriminatory that it is impossible for the affairs of the department to be conducted without criticism being forthcoming.
If we have been harsh on the minister in the last month or two it is because the minister has been so quick to rise to the defence of not only his deputy but every single person who works for the department either full time or part time. Let some member of the house, or counsel for one of the people who have been in trouble, suggest for a moment that possibly the interpreter who works part time for the department, I assume, may have left the wrong impression with one of the people involved, and the minister is immediately on his feet to tell us that neither the interpreter, any other member of the staff nor the deputy minister has ever made a mistake. He tells us that the department is perfect and always has been perfect.
I have had dealings with ministers of this department before and it is not surprising that after a minister has been on the job for eight or ten years and has worked closely with his department he comes to feel that the officials are very fine people, which they probably are, and that they do not often make mistakes. But I want to tell the minister that I 20220-2911
Interim Supply
have never known a minister before who developed this kind of departmental paralysis so fast. He has been on the job only a couple of months and already everything is perfect.
From the very beginning when these cases were first raised we have had a series of explanations, excuses and denials and even today when the minister announced he was appointing eminent counsel to look into this matter he still denied that anything was wrong was done. I suggest to him that if nothing was wrong there was no need to have an inquiry. The very fact that he has authorized an inquiry indicates that the minister finally realizes that possibly there is something which needs to be investigated. While we welcome the inquiry, I must say that I for one have a good deal of doubt about it because I am not quite clear how it will work. I am not clear whether Mr. Sedgwick is going to hold hearings, where he is going to hold the hearings or whether they are going to be held in public. I am not quite clear whether there is going to be a complete record kept of everything said, whether all the people involved are going to be heard, whether counsel for these people who have had difficulties are going to be heard, whether the press is going to be allowed to be present.
If the minister had taken the advice of the people on this side of the house who asked the questions a week ago and talked to the people who made the complaints, talked to Mr. Hooper and the lawyers who acted for these people, we would not be debating this matter today. Probably, we would not have had to have this inquiry.
I should like to raise briefly a couple of matters which the minister mentioned this afternoon when he made his statement. First of all, he left the impression with me, and I am sorry I have not the text of his address before me, that he was suggesting that possibly a good deal of the trouble was due to the fact subversive organizations are involved in these illegal entries. This is a rather serious charge. I think it ought not to be made by the minister unless he is prepared to give to the house and the country some kind of evidence of what has happened, some evidence upon which he bases this statement. If he does not, Mr. Chairman, certainly the members on this side of the house are going to treat that kind of suggestion with a great deal of scepticism.
Then, I was concerned about the minister's statement, which he has made again and again, not about whether people have been told that they could have legal aid, but his

Interim Supply
assumption that they could have legal aid, but that it was their responsibility to get that legal aid. I want to suggest that the people who are here legally, especially those about whom we have heard, are very often people who cannot speak the language. They have not got many friends and certainly have not got much money. Even if they are told they can have counsel, I think it is expecting too much to expect them to be able to get counsel.
I have before me, Mr. Chairman, the minutes of an inquiry held in the case of Mr. George Sarris on March 31, 1964. I should like to read one question put by the inquiry officer to Mr. Sarris, so the minister will understand what I am talking about. I quote:
If you so desire and at your own expense, you have the right to obtain and to be represented by counsel at this hearing.
I want to suggest that that is not good enough. A person charged with being here illegally, either at an inquiry or during court proceedings, should be able to get counsel, and he should not have to pay for it himself. I have before me, Mr. Chairman, the transcript of a court hearing in which four people, including Mr. Sarris and Mr. Thomadakis were charged-I intend to discuss this case later. This hearing was on April 10. I have the transcript here and not once during the course of these hearings were these four accused informed by the person representing the department, or the magistrate, that they were entitled to get counsel through legal aid. They were not told that if they were not ready to go ahead they could have their case postponed until they could make arrangements to get counsel. Not one of these hearings could have taken more than two or three minutes, because each one covers one page of typing, double spaced.
This afternoon the minister said that when a criminal charge is laid it is no longer the responsibility of the department. I want to take issue with that completely. I am not so concerned about the letter of the law. I believe every person is entitled to counsel. In no case where you have an indictable offence should a person appear without counsel. In a case where you are dealing with immigrants who do not have friends, do not have people to represent them, I think it is the responsibility of the department to make sure that counsel is obtained. Whether the department pays for this service or somebody else pays for it is, in my opinion, a very small matter.
I am glad we are going to have an inquiry because, after all the weeks we have been

discussing this subject, after listening to the long statement that the minister made, I still do not know to whom he spoke. He told us that everything was okay, but did he speak to anybody outside the department? Did he speak to the people who have been held for long periods of time, who have been taken to the court, charged and sentenced? Did he speak to their counsel? I think the story which counsel for the people concerned tell is entirely different from the story which the minister tells. I am not saying that the minister came into the house today or any other day and deliberately misrepresented the facts. I am suggesting however, Mr. Chairman, that there comes a time when any minister should go outside of his department so that he can get the whole story.
There are some questions which I think have to be answered, and perhaps some of the answers are in the documents the minister tabled today. I think we have to know how many people are now being held or were held in Toronto and in Montreal. I think if we look into the situation in Montreal we will find it is not much different from the situation in Toronto. How many people were held or are being held for more than a month before their hearings? What opportunity did they have to get counsel? I think it is important to look into the charge which has been made by my friend, the member for Greenwood, who has had a lot of experience in this field. He has said that very often people are told, off the record, during the inquiry, that of course they can have counsel but it really won't do them much good; they might as well get on with the job. It is a very serious thing, I think, and we need to look into this matter. Were they told not only that they could have counsel but there was counsel available without cost to them? I do not think so, because there is nothing in the transcript which would indicate this. Were they, in fact, told it would do little good to get counsel? I will come back to that a little later. Were they told it may go easier for them if they pleaded guilty? All these charges have been made either by counsel representing the people concerned or by others. These are very serious charges and I certainly hope Mr. Sedgwick will get some of the answers.
There are other things we need to know. Why are these people held in the Don jail? After all, this is looked upon as a prosperous land, a land of milk and honey and the people from the have-not countries want to come here. We cannot blame them. I am not saying we should allow all those who enter il-

legally to stay. However, if they come here, why do they have to be held in the Don jail or Bordeaux jail until their hearing is held? I understand that some of these cases take quite a long time. It has been suggested that while they are in jail awaiting their hearings they are treated just like anybody else in jail, it is assumed they are already guilty, although the trial has not yet been held and very often not even an inquiry has been held. I am told they cannot have visitors more often than a couple of times a week. I am told that the number of letters they can write is severely restricted. It seems to me this is completely unfair. It seems to me that these are questions which need to be looked into and looked into thoroughly.
Now a serious charge has been made. It has been asserted by a number of people, including a minister, Father Koulouras, who was friendly with many of these Greek seamen, that until recently when the department found people who were believed to be here illegally, a hearing was held and, if it was decided they were here illegally, they were deported quickly, and that was the end of the case. Father Koulouras claims that the whole business of charging people with a criminal offence in these circumstances began very recently. Until the practice was changed, the men apprehended were allowed bail until their cases were heard. Now Father Koulouras says, the men are being charged, which means, of course, that they have to stay here longer while they are being brought to trial, and, if found guilty, they are sentenced to periods ranging from one month to five months in jail.
I want to know what is the purpose of charging these people and sentencing them to jail. Is it true, as is being said openly in Toronto, that the department has reached the conclusion that there are a large number of people here illegally? The figure which has been mentioned-and I have heard it mentioned in more than one place-is 700. The department, it is suggested, has estimated that there are more than 700 people here illegally; the administration wishes to set an example and wants to discourage these people from coming here illegally. Is this why, instead of being deported immediately, they are being charged and sent to prison?
Another serious charge has been made by a number of these people and I hope Mr. Sedgwick will look into this. Several of them have said-I will not go into detail today, but newspaper reports have quoted them-that they were told while being questioned that
Interim Supply
if they would tell the department the names of people they know are here illegally, so that the department could apprehend those people, they would not be charged and, therefore, they would not have to serve a sentence before being deported. This charge has been made by a number of the people concerned. I can only describe it as blackmail, and I think that blackmail, whether carried on by a government or by an individual, is completely wrong and ought to be stopped. I do hope Mr. Sedgwick will look into this matter -that he will get to the bottom of it, and if this kind of tactic has been used, it will be stopped immediately.
This may be threshing old straw, but this is the kind of case which led to the Minister of Justice saying that he intended to institute an inquiry. I wish to deal, in fact, with a few of these cases which have come to light. A great deal has been made of the Hooper case. Maybe the minister feels he has been hard done by in the columns of the Toronto Telegram because he is a Liberal, and the Telegram is a Conservative newspaper. Well, I have before me an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press. If there is any newspaper which will find more reason to pat a Liberal government-any Liberal government-or any minister on the back, I do not know of one.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: It does not exist.

I wish to quote from this article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on June 1, 1964. It is headed: "Disregard of Human Rights" and it was written by Maurice Western. I wish to quote a few paragraphs just to show the minister that this affair disturbed not only members of the house and not only the Conservative papers; it became a matter of concern to everybody. I quote:
The minister made the point that Mr. Hooper was originally held in custody not only on the immigration count but also because of a charge brought by Toronto police. This was, however, withdrawn on March 15 and it is therefore indisputable that the department was solely responsible for his confinement in the Don jail for 72 days. Nor can the previous three weeks be left entirely out of the reckoning, for this time was presumably available to officials in preparing their case.
From March 15 onwards Mr. Hooper was held "undue the authority of the Immigration Act" and on March 23 the inquiry got under way. Because of his refusal to answer questions the inquiry officer adjourned the hearing to April 7 when other evidence was produced to establish his unlawful entry. Mr. Hooper was ordered deported and did not appeal.
But he was not then deported. Instead he was kept in Don jail for another 45 days while the

Interim Supply
department considered whether or not it would lay the charge which was ultimately to be dropped. Mr. Favreau on Thursday frankly conceded that there had been "certain delays" which had been "occasioned in the administrative machinery in processing this matter."
Later the paper says:
Why was Mr. Hooper without counsel while all these administrative processes were moving majestically to the climax of May 22 and anticlimax of May 25? Speaking of the situation on March 23, Mr. Favreau told the house on Thursday that "he had been given ample opportunity to retain counsel if he wished to do so".
Further on, the article states:
This does not, however, throw much light on the circumstances. Mr. Hooper is a Negro, probably of limited means. Was he aware that he could obtain legal aid? Was he assisted in finding it or left to his own resources? Mr. Brewin, a lawyer of integrity and wide experience in immigration eases claims that it is "the practice of special inquiry officers to notify people of their entitlement to the right of counsel and then tell them it is not worth their while having a counsel because in effect a decision has been made before the hearing".
Mr. Hooper's charges may be quite baseless. The fact is, however, that they cannot be tested because after these incredible delays the charge was made, only to be swiftly dropped in favour of deportation. Suspicions linger and they will not quickly be dispelled if Mr. Tremblay persists in the attitude that whatever is departmental is right. Mr. Favreau did, however, make a more favourable impression with his assurance that steps will be taken to prevent the repetition of such an occurrence in future: an assurance to which the ministry will certainly be held.
And this is from the most Liberal newspaper in Canada.
I hope the minister will reconsider some of the remarks he made on May 28 about the Hooper case when he said-and I quote:
I would state, therefore, that Mr. Hooper was held prisoner under Canadian laws and enjoyed all the privileges granted to a Canadian resident even though he is not a Canadian citizen.
If the only rights Canadians have are the kind of rights which Mr. Hooper got, then God help all of us.
I wish to deal, now, for a few moments with what I thought was a most moving plea sent to the Ontario supreme court by Mr. Thomadakis who was held in the Don jail for a long period of time. I read a few paragraphs so that they will be on the record for the future when this case is forgotten- and when more cases of this kind may occur, unless the minister takes this situation more seriously than he has done until now. I quote from the statement this man made on March 3, 1964:
On March 3, 1964, I was arrested without warrant by immigration officers. I was very co-operative an

help them as much as I could. Had I want to escape I could have as I was given opportunities by being left alone.
However, around 3.30 p.m. on March 3rd X was taken to Don jail. I was not advised of any rights and not allowed to call lawyer. I did not know what I was charged with and did not make an appearance in court or before any authority.
Two days later the immigration come to see me and question me about how I come to Canada. They did not tell me any rights or that I could have lawyer.
I do not speak English very well and the jail authorities did not help me to understand my position. On 3rd or 4th of April the R.C.M.P. came and tell me why I was arrested for the first time.
Here again we have a period of five or six weeks:
On April 9, 1964, I got a letter saying I would go to court next day. I had not chance to get in touch with anyone as the letter came in afternoon and jail regulations say I must put in requests in the morning.
No one told about legal aid. I have great trouble explaining things to the guards and everyone says it doesn't matter. I went to court on April 10 (38 days after my arrest) for the first time.
I had no lawyer and interpreter for immigration told me to plead guilty and I go home.
I want to interject for a minute and point this out to the minister. This is what Mr. Thomadakis says; I repeat it:
-interpreter for immigration told me to plead guilty and I go home, If I make trouble and plead not guilty I go back to jail until the case comes up again and maybe I get a heavy prison sentence. I plead guilty but I still do not understand.
Even if Mr. Thomadakis is not completely right, the very fact that an illegal immigrant, 21 years of age, who does not know the language, thinks this is what happened to him is, I think, an insult to the kind of justice which this country provides. The minister on a number of occasions has said that he checked into this particular case and that this did not happen. I asked the minister-and Hansard will show this was done three weeks or more ago-to contact the lawyer for Mr. Thomadakis, and the minister rejected my suggestion. I was not as squeamish as the minister; I called Mr. Mintz, who has acted for a number of these people, and here are the notes that I made of that conversation. Mr. Mintz said that he got in touch with the interpreter. He said that the interpreter said she told Mr. Thomadakis, "You can plead guilty or you will be found guilty; and if you want to get things over quickly, you had better plead guilty". I am not saying the minister knew this is what the interpreter was saying, but I am saying these whole procedures need to be looked into.

The same day on which Mr. Thomadakis was convicted in court a Mr. Georgios Sarris appeared in the same court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, could I ask the hon. gentleman a question? I understand that the hon. gentleman is now speaking of the proceedings before the court; is that right? Was this the interpreter who interpreted to that immigrant before the court, or is the hon. member referring to the proceedings before the board of inquiry?
This is the interpreter who acted in court. What I said was that Mr. Mintz quoted her as advising Mr. Thomadakis to this effect. It was not said in court; it was said before the court proceedings.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I put a further question, Mr. Chairman? Is the hon. gentleman aware that the interpreter in court is an officer of the court and of the province; he is not an officer of the immigration department or any other department of the federal government. Is the hon. member also aware that normally if a judge is not sure whether a plea of guilty is motivated by the proper factors, it is he who normally must inquire into the reason for the plea of guilty, and the judge is free to accept or refuse the plea of guilty. But one thing that ought to be made clear is that from the moment a person is before a court under the jurisdiction of the province, the officers of the court are within the authority of the province, and not of the federal government; and the proceedings, as far as the plea of guilty is concerned, are within the authority of the judge himself. It might make some difference.

I do not know what difference it would make to Mr. Thomadakis or to Mr. Sarris whether the people they were appearing before represented the federal government, the immigration department, the Department of Justice or the provincial government. In the final analysis, the end result was the same; they wound up in jail. I do not think it makes a hoot of difference who was responsible. I am sure that the Minister of Justice, who has a great number of tasks to perform, has seen this transcript; but if he has not, I will be glad to send it over to him. This is a transcript of the proceedings in which these four people were concerned. And I repeat what I said earlier, namely that the whole proceedings could not have taken more than 15 minutes. Nobody-not the representative of the department, not the magistrate or anybody else asked these people if they understood what was going on. No-
Interim Supply
body asked them if they had counsel. Nobody asked them if they knew they could have counsel.
What difference does it make whose responsibility it was I have said before, and I say it again-and perhaps we will have more success with the Minister of Justice than we have had with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration up till now-that I think it is our responsibility to make sure these people are properly represented. We should take a leaf from the decisions made recently by the United States supreme court, to the effect that every person in every case involving an indictable offence is entitled to counsel, and if they do not have counsel they cannot get a fair trial. I think we should stop splitting these legal hairs; I am not too concerned about that aspect of the matter and I will leave this to my legal friends, who do a very good job. But I am interested in seeing that these people receive some kind of justice, because they did not get it and they are still not getting it.
There has been some question about how old Mr. Sarris was, but I think it is now established that he was not more than 17 years old when he appeared before the magistrate. He was 15 years old when he committed the offence of entering this country illegally. He was 16 when he was apprehended. He was, as I say, the ripe age of 17 when he was convicted. I wonder what purpose there was in giving Mr. Sarris a jail sentence. Could he not have been simply deported, because he was guilty? He pleaded guilty. This would have solved that problem. But no, he had to get a jail sentence.
The minister said on one occasion that there were only six people who had been held more than 30 days. I am speaking from memory now. The Telegram, on the basis of information given to them by Mr. Mintz, who has been counsel for many of these people, had a list of about 22 people. I hope the correct information is in those documents which the minister tabled today.
I want to deal with one more matter, Mr. Chairman, and then finish by reading from a letter which the minister received. I do this to show that this kind of thing cannot help but bring our kind of justice into contempt. This case was reported in the Toronto newspapers on June 16 in which three people were brought before the magistrate and were permitted to go free until their trial, on bail of $500. The three people are Nick Polycratis, Peter Theodorou and Steve Kafouros. Bail was put up for them by a Mr. Bassel, acting

on behalf of the Greek-Canadian congress. Each of the three men was given his clothing and taken upstairs. But in each case the immigration department still had a hold order in force

so back down to the cells they went-

I am sure the Minister of Justice could again read quite a lecture on how they were given bail and how these were proceedings against them in a criminal court; but the provisions of the Immigration Act, which we are going to discuss on another occasion, do not give the minister or the department the right to hold people in this way, and I am sure the minister thinks these people must have been very confused. I am sure they did not know which side was up by the time the magistrate had finished with them. To be told by a magistrate that they were free to go on bail, and then to be told they could not go until hours or days later, must certainly have been confusing.
I want to finish up by putting on the record a letter sent to the minister by Mr. Mintz and Mr. Weisdorf, both of whom work for the legal aid organization in Toronto and have had a good deal more experience with this kind of case than I. Their experience has been both hard and bitter. I will just quote a few paragraphs from the letter which they sent to the minister, which I think summarizes the situation better than I could:
We request an admission from Mr. Tremblay that he recognizes the excesses carried out under the harsh, dictatorial provisions of the Immigration Act by his administrative officers.
Once this is conceded, the government should convene a royal commission to investigate the prevention of administrative excess in the future -either in the form of an amended Immigration Act, or in a uniform code of procedure for all administrative officers and tribunals, or in the institution of the office of ombudsman.
The abuses which the legal aid department has recently brought to light are certainly not limited to the department of immigration, but occur on every level of industry and government.
CMr. Orlikow.]
Wherever employees of any organization are given untrammelled power, unchecked by the judiciary and hidden from the light of public opinion, injustice is bound to occur.
Mr. Chairman, I will end on those words to the minister and I hope that he will pay some attention to them in the next few weeks.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to deliver a lecture for the benefit of the hon. member for Winnipeg North, first of all because I am not too good at that sort of thing and I am afraid that having not taught at university for quite a few years I have probably lost touch with teaching. But one thing I do want to say, which is in no way intended to do away with any responsibility that any federal department may have, is that because of the division of responsibilities-I will not say powers, because I hate the use of that word under the British North America Act-between the federal government and the provincial governments it so happens that in the course of a few weeks or months one and the same person has to cope with authorities which in certain phases are federal and in certain phases are provincial.
The hon. gentleman was referring a few minutes ago to what happened to one person whose case went before the courts. The reason I raise the matter is because the interpreter involved was surely not a federal officer, and could not be given instructions by the federal Department of Citizenship and Immigration or the Department of Justice. Therefore, it was up to the court to decide whether or not, in view of the fact that this detainee was not perfectly possessed of either the French or English language, which are the two official languages of this country, he was not totally conversant with the consequences of his decision in deciding to plead guilty.
All I mean by that is that in a series of facts and circumstances one must try to ascribe responsibility to the proper authority. I do not mean to say that there was any wrong act or action on the part of the provincial authorities; I am not the judge of that. But surely it is important when dealing with a man who at certain moments falls within the jurisdiction of provincial authorities and at other moments falls within the jurisdiction of the federal authorities, not to charge the federal authorities only with the whole of the responsibility because the person concerned happened to have entered Canada illegally and is faced with the application of the Immigration Act.

I should like to give an example of this, and it is a converse example. The administration of justice in the provinces rests with the attorneys general of the provinces. Very often an attorney general, because of a conviction entered in one case, causes the person who has been prosecuted by him and who is condemned to more than two years in prison to be sent a federal penitentiary. From the moment that person enters the federal penitentiary it is surely no more the responsibility of the attorney general of the province to see to it that this man be treated according to standards otherwise applicable while he is within the confines of the penitentiary. It is up to the federal commissioner of penitentiaries and to the latter's subordinate officer to see to it that the proper standards be applied; and I say that from that moment on nobody could say that there is an onus upon that attorney general of the province, he having carried out his duty as attorney general and sent that person to the penitentiary, to see to it that that person in the penitentiary be dealt with according to the provisions of the bill of rights, or otherwise. This does not deny any of the responsibilities which under the federal statutes lie with the appropriate minister of any federal department, including myself.
Both the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and myself have shown to what extent it is important that we must be satisfied in our own minds that we have been or will be discharging in the future our responsibilities in the most complete fashion. This has been proven, if you like, by the appointment of Mr. Sedgwick as counsel as early as last Friday, with the relatively broad terms of reference which were given to him. I mean by this that one must always be careful not to give the impression that all of the evils which might happen to a man must be blamed upon the department which, at one moment in that man's life, happened to have been dealing with him.
On the whole, Mr. Chairman, I must say, and I know the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration shares my view that we are all indebted to the hon. members in this house, because I know this is the only context in which these suggestions must be taken, for their co-operation in directing our attention to certain cases, which of course could not have been brought to the attention of the minister before or were not part of the minister's knowledge before. We should also like to thank them for making suggestions, which illustrates once more the importance 20220-292
Interim Supply
of this great institution, the House of Commons, which by the method of questions, remarks, comments or statements, makes for a better and always more human administration, both of justice and the statutes of this country.

Would the minister permit a question. I understand that the minister is recognizing another member who contributed to this debate, and although I should like to take part later in the debate I would like to ask a question now. Although it is true, as he says, that the administration of justice is a provincial responsibility, in cases such as immigration cases where the prosecution is initiated by the department and in which they are responsible to that extent for bringing the immigrant to court, is there any reason the minister can suggest why the department should not take the responsibility of seeing that the immigrant is in fact properly instructed as to his rights, has access to counsel, and has knowledge of the case to be made against him?
Does not the minister think that the good name and reputation of Canada require that the federal department, which initiates these prosecutions of persons for illegal entry into Canada, should also take the responsibility to see the legal proceedings which ensue are such that they are a credit to Canada, rather than the sort of thing we have been hearing about in the last few weeks?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The remark just made by the hon. member corresponds to quite an exact degree with the statement made this afternoon by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, when he said he thought this particular measure was one that deserved very serious and thorough consideration. The only reason I made the remark was because the very act which was charged against one particular officer, that is, the interpreter in the case concerned-which was a positive act- could surely not be controlled at that moment by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration or by the Department of Justice. But I agree we will have to go into this very serious question, the question of the general instructions at the very inception of a case, both to counsel and otherwise.

Does the Minister of Justice think that, if the federal department of citizenship had provided counsel, any such problem would have arisen with interpreters?

Interim. Supply

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not catch the latter part of the question.

Does this not point up the need for the federal government, through its Department of Citizenship and Immigration, to provide counsel to these citizens, or quasi citizens, so that problems with interpreters will not arise? Do the arguments the minister is using not point up the federal responsibility?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that would be a strict matter of opinion. I do not think there is responsibility incumbent upon the government, if everybody concerned at all levels performed their duty in a full and complete fashion; but I can only repeat that human beings being what they are, they are susceptible to error, and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration was right in stating this afternoon that this was a matter to which he was bent on giving serious consideration.

Mr. Chairman, some time ago, I was surprised to learn that an important plant in the city of Joliette, that of the Consolidated Textile, which provides jobs to quite a few family heads, had decided to put aside its $3 million expansion project and transfer it to Alexandria, in the province of Ontario. That plant, which is already in operation in Joliette, was to add to its present establishment a weaving and dyeing plant which would have employed more than 200 persons.
The city of Joliette and the province of Quebec are losing this building project valued at $3 million, because the company would rather carry it out in an area designated as economically weak by the federal government, to benefit from tax incentives, that is, tax exemptions and benefits to be gained therefrom. That policy was announced by the federal government and particularly by the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury).
In the Joliette area, there are already over
4,000	unemployed persons. As Joliette is not designated as a depressed area according to federal government standards, it follows that the province of Quebec and the city of Joliette are losing an important factory which employed more than 200 people.
I protest on behalf of the people of the county of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm who surely do not deserve such punishment from the government. The people of my constituency pay taxes just as the people of any other constituency in the country, and I be-

lieve that this decision of the government to designate certain areas in the country as depressed areas, where factories benefit from tax exemptions, is detrimental to the economy of the Joliette region.
Mr. Chairman, several members are surprised by the revolution which is smouldering at the present time in French Canada and more especially in the province of Quebec. I can tell you that I am surprised that such a revolution, or unrest, did not take place 40 or 50 years ago. One of the reasons why the province of Quebec is the setting for that unrest is certainly that, from the economic viewpoint, it lags behind all the others. Therefore, the Quebec people want to make up for lost time and they are trying to find a formula to improve their economy.
Let me point out that the standard of living of the Quebec citizen is 10 per cent lower than that of the average Canadian and 27 per cent lower than that of the Ontario citizen.
We barely control 5 per cent of the economic activity of Canada, while our ethnic group represents 29 per cent of the population. In the province of Quebec itself, our group forms about 82.6 per cent of the population, but only controls 10 per cent of the economic activity, while we hold only 20 per cent of the key positions.
Mr. Chairman, about 40 per cent of the unemployed in Canada live in Quebec and the average income per capita in 1963 amounted approximately to $1,700 while it reached $2,000 in Ontario and $2,600 in the United States. While France and Belgium experienced heavy losses during the last world war, the average income per capita was $1,750 and $1,850.
Mr. Chairman, I can go on. The average income of the Quebec farmer is less than $1,200 per year.
In view of this situation the people of Quebec are justified in being concerned and in getting agitated so as to stir public opinion.
As for the federal government, the province of Quebec does not get its fair share. As a matter of fact, it only has 11 per cent of the railways built in Canada, and the federal government has cancelled the proposed building of a railway in the Gaspe peninsula, which would surely have provided a means of restoring economy in that part of our province.
On the federal level, French speaking Canadians do not get their fair share within the federal civil service. French speaking Canadians must be bilingual, whereas the other

element in our country only has to know one language.
In the province of Quebec, the rights of the minorities are respected. As a matter of fact, the English speaking minority enjoys the same rights, in the field of education, as the French speaking majority, whereas in most of the other provinces, the French speaking minority does not share equal rights with the English speaking majority.
The province of Quebec has contributed greatly to our country's development. It never lagged behind and, during the last world war, Quebec gave more soldiers, more of its children, to the Canadian army, proportionately speaking, than the other provinces. It did its share not only in men but also in money for peace.
Moreover, it must be remembered that from 1942 to 1947, Ottawa received $2,258,381,000 from Quebec and gave it back only $103 million. That shows, therefore, that the province of Quebec also did its war effort. It sacrificed a large share of its rights to enable the federal government to get the necessary income for its war effort and the maintenance of peace.
Mr. Chairman, the St. Jean Baptiste societies recently held an important convention in the province of Quebec. They adopted rather strong, energetic and categorical resolutions concerning the future of our country. Now, they feel that the time has come not only to revise our constitution, but to call all the provinces to a conference in order to find a definite solution and to give recognition to the existence of two free nations, both of which would carry out their destiny while remaining closely associated. In other words, Mr. Chairman, they would be in favour of convening a federal-provincial conference in the future to consider the possibility of setting up two national states if the majority of the people from Quebec-
And two parties.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Lamontagne) just made a remark which I did not hear. I would be very happy if he would repeat it.
And two parties.

Perhaps the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean helped, by his centralizing theories, the change and the revolution which is going on in the province of Quebec. And everybody knows what the elite of that province thinks of his new brilliant formula, 20220-292J
Interim, Supply
co-operative federalism. People know what Mr. Rene Levesque and many citizens of the province of Quebec and even of the country think of it.
Even the member for Three Rivers.

And it is probably this lucky find on the part of the Secretary of State, which induced the federation of the St. Jean Baptiste societies to draw this conclusion that it would be preferable if there were two associate states in Canada instead of a single federal state.
Mr. Chairman, I am always surprised to hear the English speaking members in this house wonder about the province of Quebec. They should not be worried, and if there is presently a revolution in the province of Quebec, this definitely concerns the inhabitants of the province of Quebec. I do not say that the inhabitants of the other provinces should not have a look at what goes on in the province of Quebec, but if the inhabitants of the other provinces and my English speaking colleagues really want to work in the interests of confederation, they simply have to advise their provincial governments to follow the example set by the province of Quebec in its handling of the English speaking minority in that province.
A great uneasiness prevailing in Canada at the present time certainly comes from failure to recognize our rights in regard to language and religious teaching in the provinces other than the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, reference is made to national unity. People want a strong nation, but two bills are introduced in the house asking us to accept at the same time a maple leaf flag and the union jack.
Mr. Chairman, such a formula is not acceptable for the people of the province of Quebec, who want only one distinctive flag. On that flag, they want no symbol of the past, no fleur-de-lis, but they want a national distinctive flag, no matter if it has one or three maple leaves.
It is not that the province of Quebec does not hold the union jack or the red ensign in some veneration, but it will always object to the choice of a symbol other than a national distinctive flag.
Mr. Chairman, in two days, the French Canadians will celebrate their national day. Let me read an advertisement published in the newspaper Le Devoir this morning and paid for by Henry Morgan Company Limited, a large English store in the province of Quebec:

Interim Supply
-and finally, since the sun was married with the fleur-de-lis as a modem sign of the French renewal in Quebec, it is no longer permitted to doubt, not of our survival, but of our living which is already radiant, brilliant and intensive.
Let us think of the 1,200 immigrants of the early days of the colony who developed to the point that they make up a people of some 5 or 6 million French Canadians forming a young, dynamic and forward-looking nation. French Canada, a living reality.
Mr. Chairman, in my opinion there are two nations in Canada, and I believe that French Canadians are numerous enough in this country to be considered a nation. This is what I believe, and I hope that the government will, as soon as possible, examine the important suggestions made by the St. Jean Baptiste society of the province of Quebec.
Canada should fully understand that we have to reach a compromise, to remake our Canadian constitution and, if necessary, in order to save Canada from annexation by the United States, recognize two associated states, which might have their own responsibilities and co-operate in the interest of this country's economy.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm a question?
Yes.
Mr. Chairman, if I understood the hon. member rightly, he said that we, in Quebec, do not want to preserve any symbol of our past. Those are his exact words-
Excuse me-
Would you agree to the French language-which is also a symbol of our past-being completely abandoned, and a new language being spoken in the province of Quebec?

Mr. Chairman, I think that the hon. member for Lake St. John understood me. First of all, the French language is certainly not a symbol. When I was speaking of symbols, I meant flags. I said that the majority, at least 99 per cent of the people in the province of Quebec want a distinctive flag without any trace of the past. That is what they want, and that is what I said.

Mr. Chairman, I want to return to the subject of immigration. I regard it as one of very great importance because, although this is not always recognized, the good name and reputation of Canada through-
[Mr. Pigeon.)
out the world hinges to some extent upon the way that we in Canada through our immigration department treat those who come from all parts of the world. We know that they come to Canada from every part of the world at the present time. Very often they return to those countries, and the ideas they get of the administration of Canadian justice, the fairness of our laws, the consideration, kindness and understanding of the officials that they meet, are the hallmarks by which they judge Canada as a whole. Therefore, I make no apology for returning to this subject although I hope not to repeat what has been said earlier in the debate or to repeat some of the matters I have discussed on other occasions.
First of all, I should like to say at once that so far as I am concerned I do not propose to take part in any attack upon the minister or upon the staff which advises him. It is natural, as has been said, that in his department he should be subjected to a great deal of criticism. Personally, I have found both this minister and other ministers considerate, careful and conscientious about the individual cases that are drawn to their attention. I have absolutely no complaint whatever to make about the individual approach of the minister to these problems.
Having said that, I want to say at once that basically in the administration of our immigration, the system is rotten. I use the words "rotten system"-they may be strong words- advisedly and carefully. I must confess my disappointment that the minister, in making the announcement he has made, was not able to tell this house that certain positive steps were going to be taken. I appreciate the fact that the advice of an eminent lawyer such as Mr. Sedgwick will be helpful to the department. Knowing Mr. Sedgwick, and knowing the department, I hope that out of that advice will come certain worth-while things. However, no advice from a lawyer is going to substitute for the department itself deciding to go to the very root of the problem of immigration by deciding whether or not the would-be immigrant is, in fact, to have what parliament itself has said is required, namely a fair hearing under the act. I have said the system is a rotten system because the basic right to know the case that is made against you, the basic right to be able to defend yourself against hidden aspersions, is denied in practice.
The Immigration Act provides, as the minister well knows, a series of sections that entitle the would-be immigrant to a hearing.

My friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North, has spoken about the need for having counsel. I have been counsel in hundreds of these cases. I tell the minister and I tell anybody who wants to listen, that the right to counsel itself is meaningless unless counsel, by some system that can be evolved can find out what is the basis of the objection to the admission of the person in question or, alternatively, why they are now being put out of the country. As long as we have what I can only describe as "phony" reasons such as, "You have not got a visa" or "You have not got a medical certificate", then an individual will not have a fair hearing. The department says: We will not tell you why; those are the reasons.
I do not know if the minister has at his fingertips how many immigration cases have been disposed of out of those 30 a week, on the grounds that "You do not have a visa" or "You do not have a medical certificate". I suspect the very large percentage of cases are being disposed of on these grounds. I say to the minister and to the house, therefore, that those grounds are virtually meaningless, because if you then inquire why the the person has not got a visa, why they refuse him a visa, they will not tell you. There may be some sort of police record that has been secured from the country of origin. There may be some health condition about which you do not know, which has been revealed on a medical examination. There may be innumerable reasons, good, bad or indifferent. However, behind this screen of reasons that are not given, any sort of discriminatory reason that an individual officer may have could operate to keep a would-be immigrant out of the country.
Does the minister feel any sense of justice0 Could I feel any sense of justice if I wanted to bring my brother to this country from Italy or wherever he may be when I am told he cannot come because he does not have a visa? Why has he not got a visa? The department says, "We will not let you".
I do not know what the reason is, but they do not tell you the real reason for not admitting a person. I say, therefore, that until the immigration department or Mr. Sedgwick, or anybody else, make up their minds to the fact that those who apply for admission to this country or who wish to bring their relatives into this country are entitled to a sort of basic hearing, the situation will not be rectified. I am not asking for a legal hearing where the evidence is disclosed in detail, but only for the basic elements of a fair hear-

The reason I say it should be applied-I know there are difficulties-is that it would first of all enable the immigrant and his family to recognize that they have had justice. In addition, it would enable them, in many cases, to dispose of the objections that have been made. I have been fortunate enough in some cases in which I represented an immigrant to be told by the minister the reason for the objection, after all the proceedings were over. The minister has been good enough to say, "Well, this is the reason". Then, I have had a chance to look into the reason and find out that the reason was not of great substance. I have been able to persuade the minister to change his mind. This is fine; but this course is not available to the average person. This right to meet the objection is not available except in cases where the person is able to get a member of parliament or a qualified lawyer to take up his case.
It looks as though it were ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman. I have a few observations to make and I would prefer to make them tomorrow, -if it is ten o'clock.
