REPORTED SPEECH IN BRITAIN BY ARNOLD HEENEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 28, 1963, we find that on page 5199 of Hansard the Secretary of

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) is reported as saying this during a debate on external affairs:
The nurturing of one of our cornerstones of foreign policy, the commonwealth, is a basic feature of our external policies. In the past few years membership has been progressively enlarged until today it embraces 16 sovereign states. The majority now are in Asia and in Africa. It is because of the special insight which the commonwealth gives us into the new forces which have emerged in the post-war era that we most value this unique association of states. The commonwealth practice of continuing consultation among members on matters of mutual concern is especially valuable in a world in which race and colour have too often tended to be divisive forces.
We can well imagine the minister making that statement with the organ-like clarity of voice which prompted one Texan visitor in the galleries on one occasion to go out and ask a member of the protective staff: "What is the name of that cathedral?"
In any event, I was horrified, on Friday, to pick up a copy of the Ottawa Citizen and see on the front page an article entitled "Commonwealth slipping-Heeney". It was written by Charles King and it went as follows:
London-Canada's former ambassador in Washington today rejected the commonwealth as a "meaningful'' political reality.
He argued: "Whatever the future of the commonwealth, it can no longer be centred on London, nor, for the great majority of its members, clustered round the monarchy.
Just two weeks before commonwealth prime ministers gather in London for an important conference, Arnold Heeney delivered his blockbuster to a British audience assembled by the Ditchley foundation, which calls itself "an active educational centre for British-Amerlcan understanding."
Then the chairman of the Canadian section of the international joint commission had this to say-and it is in quotes:
It seems to me unprofitable.. .to place undue emphasis nowadays on friendship and special relationship within the commonwealth. The winds of change.. .have laid bare the dry and brittle roots of much cherished doctrine.
It is obvious enough that the commonwealth cannot recover nor achieve any meaningful degree of political cohesion. Nor does it seem likely that our economic relations will become much closer.
Now, in view of the minister's announcement of this government's policy with respect to the commonwealth, and after reading this article by such an important civil servant-a man who, I am informed, has never been known to express a single opinion on anything outside the minister's office previously, except on the weather-I was moved to ask the hon. gentleman this question: "Would the minister inform the house if that statement

is a reflection of government policy and, if not, what right has this servant of the public to be making statements in contradiction of government policy?"
This matter was also brought to my attention by a number of other people who were certainly shocked at this statement by Mr. Arnold Heeney as reported from London, in contradiction to the attitude taken by this government toward the commonwealth. I am sure all of us here take strong exception to Mr. Heeney's opinion with respect to the present and future value of the commonwealth of nations of which we are a member.
I do not know how much more time I have. I have a number of authorities here, but I shall not have a chance to quote them. However, I have brought one particularly interesting authority with me and I should like to read briefly from page 12 of Lecture Series No. 2. This is from a lecture delivered at the University of British Columbia:
The official does not make decisions. His responsibilities fall into two categories. First, it is his duty to inform and advise the political authority- usually the minister of his department. In the words of A.D.P. Heeney, himself one of the most distinguished of Canadian civil servants: "Decision is the prerogative of the minister."
Now I am quoting Mr. Heeney against Mr. Heeney. He goes on to say:
But the expert must stick to his last. He must appreciate the limitations of his office. He must appreciate the limitations of his own expert knowledge. He has neither the experience nor the special kind of wisdom-let alone the authority-to govern.
The second duty of the civil servant is to carry out the tasks imposed by the policy of the government, that is, to administer the law. President Cleveland summarized it in the single sentence: "Public officers are the servants and agents of the people, to execute the laws which the people have made."
I have drawn this matter to the attention of the house. I see my time has practically expired. I look forward to an explanation from the Secretary of State for External Affairs in answer to the questions I have raised.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion and false in the impression it conveys". Among other things, that report describes Mr. Heeney as a former Canadian ambassador to London, which of course is incorrect on two grounds. In London we have a high commissioner, not an ambassador; and Mr. Heeney has never held that post. Mr. Heeney, in defence of his own position, calls the report "a distortion of what I had to say in a lecture of some 45 minutes from a carefully prepared text on the subject 'Friends and relations: A Canadian perspective on Anglo-American affairs' ". Mr. Heeney's telegram also says, "You are fully aware of my attachment to the commonwealth, and in fact this emerges from the text itself." I note that at page 12 of the text Mr. Heeney says:
So. we Canadians assert a very special relationship with you in Britain, one hallowed by blood and treasured at every stage of our development from colony to nation, embracing within its friendly circle many principal elements in our national life, crowned by the monarchy itself.
